versions.body:
# Web Quota and Native Negotiation Proposal

First, break this interface discussion into separate notes. One question is whether the web storage namespace can actually store data independently; another is how much of the old native-module entry can still be retained during runtime negotiation. Neither should be closed out based solely on "backend availability."

The current proposal is to treat the web entry as a backend boundary that can be tried independently. Creation should accept `namespace` and `quotaBytes`. When a write exceeds the limit, the caller needs an explicit failure, rather than allowing data already present in the same scope to change as a result. The record provisionally uses `QUOTA_EXCEEDED` to represent capacity rejection, but how the error object is returned has not been decided.

The experiment should not only check whether the object is created successfully. Prepare two differently named scopes, leave data in one first, and then try writing content expected to exceed capacity to that scope; use the other only for comparison. After the failure, read from the original scope again. Do not switch to a new object to determine whether contamination occurred. The return form of `read` still needs to be confirmed against the existing backend.

The old native-module should not be turned into a second storage implementation at this stage. It is more like a negotiation layer: at runtime, first determine whether the existing module can provide the capabilities required by the request, then decide whether to retain a compatibility view. Finding that the module exists does not mean it is already suitable to handle the request.

The inspection entry point noted here is `packages/async-storage/src/runtime/MemoryBackend.js`. It can be used to identify the existing backend's objects used for storing and retrieving data and its adjacent operations, but it cannot by itself prove web isolation or replace assessment of the old module's capabilities.

Open questions: data ownership when no name is passed; capacity accounting; whether to still return a compatibility view when the old module lacks the required capabilities; how to show both that the previous data is still present and that this write had no effect.

# Web Quotas and Native Negotiation Proposal

The web namespace and the legacy native-module were initially placed in the same interface sketch because both go through runtime selection. On review, combining them this way was not appropriate: the former concerns data boundaries within the same type of backend; the latter concerns whether a compatibility entry point should continue to participate when its capabilities are insufficient. These two issues can share a creation entry point, but not success criteria.

## Positions Left in the Draft

An old record contains this sentence: "Have the web path follow the in-memory backend's instance relationships first, and add isolation later." It is retained to explain why the review at the time only looked at successful creation. It can no longer serve as a basis for the trial. Getting an object from creation does not show that two namespaces cannot read each other's data or compete for capacity; likewise, discovering the legacy module does not show that it is suitable for handling this request.

Another idea at the time was to make the capacity limit a caller convention: callers would estimate the content size first and not call the backend if the estimate exceeded the limit. This approach was not pursued. There was no common decision point between estimation and the actual write, and different callers would also end up applying inconsistent criteria. If a capacity boundary exists, the selected web backend should own it; callers should only receive the result.

Another unresolved question was whether all web instances without an explicit name could share a default scope, with names used only as debug labels. This would cost less to integrate, but would leave callers to interpret isolation: two instances could appear to have different names while reading across each other's data underneath. The sketch no longer treats this as the default direction; how the default name should be interpreted remains undecided.

## Observation Order for the Test Cases

The trial focuses on two inputs after creation: `namespace` and `quotaBytes`. The former assigns data to a storage scope; the latter limits the amount of writes that scope is allowed to accept. Cross-platform migration is out of scope here, and the presence of the legacy module is not used to infer whether web storage is available.

Prepare two distinct namespaces. First, retain committed data in one of them, then submit a write to that same namespace that is expected to exceed the limit. Use the other namespace only to observe isolation, not to contribute to the capacity total. This at least separates three questions: whether existing data is retained, whether this write is accepted, and whether the other namespace is affected. Failures continue to use `QUOTA_EXCEEDED`, but the error structure has not been settled.

Do not use an empty read alone as evidence of rejection. An empty value could result from having no prior data, using the wrong name, getting the instance from a different source, or reading a different target. The review record must at least state what existed before the write, which scope the attempt targeted, and which object was read again after the failure. If `read` fails, retain the backend error context as well; do not leave only a generic exception with no indication of its source.

Capacity limits and key overwrites are not the same thing. If a test case only writes the same key repeatedly, the final state cannot tell us whether capacity is measured by final content, by write operations, or is not enforced at this layer at all. Test cases should therefore not combine overwriting an existing key and adding new content into a single judgment. No specific measurement rule is assumed here; the rule needs to be confirmed jointly through the implementation and the interface documentation.

## An Inconclusive Look Back

Someone later revisited `packages/async-storage/src/runtime/MemoryBackend.js` via the creation entry point and confirmed that this location was suitable for continuing to trace the existing backend's surrounding read/write paths. That inspection did not, however, make it a basis for implementing web isolation. The sketch originally cited "the in-memory backend exists" as evidence that "web isolation can reuse it"; that claim is now marked obsolete. The file location can only help navigate back to the backend object under discussion; it cannot replace a comparison of the two namespaces.

The review also exposed an easy source of confusion: if a different object is used to read after the write, there is no way to tell whether an empty value comes from rejection, a different name, or a different read target. The comparison must return to the same scope and retain the content that existed before the attempt. This order is intended to distinguish the failed operation from the prior state, not to prescribe every backend's internal implementation in advance.

Someone suggested putting both namespaces into a complex batch and checking everything at once. That suggestion was not adopted. A batch would introduce ordering and partial-failure issues at the same time, whereas the first task here is to confirm the name and capacity boundaries. Once those are mixed into a batch, any exception could be explained as batch processing rather than a namespace relationship.

## Legacy Module Negotiation

The legacy native-module path should not promise to take over all requests automatically. It is only meaningful when, at runtime, it can satisfy the capabilities required for this creation request. If its capabilities are insufficient, the creation path needs to provide an explainable selection result rather than silently redirecting the request to an object with different behavior.

One option considered was to have the compatibility entry point return a "best-effort" view even when negotiation failed, to reduce the changes needed by legacy callers. This idea was not retained as a trial objective. Once callers receive an object, they can easily interpret "the object exists" as "all subsequent operations can be relied on." If recovery or another path is unsupported, the failure will be deferred to a point where it is harder to locate.

Strict rejection and retaining a permissive view each have costs. Strict rejection exposes dependencies on the legacy entry point earlier, but avoids presenting a non-equivalent object as equivalent. A permissive view can defer migration, but mixes selection failures with subsequent read/write failures. At this stage, only silent substitution is ruled out; no conclusion is being set in advance for either strategy.

## Conditions for Continuing

Expand this trial only when the following questions can be answered independently: can the two namespaces be distinguished; was this write left uncommitted after exceeding capacity; and, when the legacy module lacks the required capabilities, can the creator tell that selection did not succeed? If answering any one of these still requires guessing where an instance came from, do not call the interface stable.

If capacity checks affect previously committed data, or unexplained cross-namespace reads or writes occur, stop expanding the web entry point. If legacy module negotiation disguises failure as a successful view, stop recommending that entry point to legacy callers and clarify the selection result first.

versions.body:
# Web Quotas and Native Negotiation Proposal

This draft has never been renamed, yet it contains several rounds of different questions. The earliest margin note only said, "Can web be listed separately, and can the legacy module continue negotiating?" It was only later that we realized these two phrases could easily lead people to assume that both were asking whether a backend exists. In fact, they concern different things: one is about which scope the data lands in and what that scope retains after a failure; the other is about whether the runtime can explain why it selected or did not select the legacy entry point.

This page was not originally a complete interface specification, but rather working notes comparing two integration points side by side. Later additions did not erase the sequence of events, because the early observation that "it can be created" really did skew the order of checks. The candidates, withdrawn wording, sample reviews, and opinions from the review panel are retained below; together, they explain why the current trial no longer treats the two branches as a single success assertion.

## 2023-06-26 11:12: Drafting only confirmed that the entry point was worth retaining

The goal during drafting was narrow: the creation path could select web, the storage object could have a name, and the backend would reject capacity overages; the legacy native-module was treated as a compatibility source that might continue negotiating. At that time, "rejection" had not been articulated in terms of a commit boundary, nor had anyone discussed how existing data should be retained. The examples in the record only required that two instances with different names could be created, so they could show only that the entry parameters were worth testing further, not that the data was isolated.

The early draft was also overly optimistic about the legacy module. Once the legacy module was found, preserving it wherever possible seemed likely to reduce changes for legacy callers. This judgment did not distinguish between "the module can be found" and "the module can provide the capabilities required for this creation." The latter only later became the center of the dispute. The old record did not answer what the creator should receive when capabilities were insufficient, nor did it explain exactly which operations were promised once the compatibility view was obtained.

There were three unresolved items at the time: which scope the data should belong to when no name was provided; how capacity should be interpreted; and what the creator should receive when the legacy module could not handle the request. They were raised repeatedly during several later checks, but there were no answers during drafting. The blank is preserved here rather than backfilling the later resolution into the earlier stage.

One scope constraint has remained in effect: all backends will not be rewritten for this trial. The web entry point first needs to establish its own local boundaries, while existing backends serve only as comparison targets. If all backends were brought in from the outset, every observation would be drowned out by implementation differences, making it impossible to answer the question of how web's own names and capacity relate.

## 2023-06-26: The old margin-note approach, now deprecated

A margin note from after the initial draft once said: the web layer could first reuse existing in-memory objects; as long as the objects were created separately, they could provisionally be treated as isolated; the capacity issue could be refined after the integrating side reported an error. This passage was not removed from the document because it explains why some people later compared only newly created objects.

That judgment no longer applies. Creating objects separately does not mean they have separate data scopes, nor does it mean that capacity checks will not affect content already present in the objects. It mistakenly treats "number of objects" as "data boundaries" and also pushes failure handling onto callers. Subsequent review did not support this inference; instead, it forced the discussion back to the data state that should be compared directly.

During the same period, a more permissive candidate also emerged: have all web instances without explicit names share a default scope, with names used only for debugging. This is simple to integrate in the short term, but it would allow two seemingly different instances to read across each other. It was not adopted as the default approach. Here, we still do not draw a conclusion about the default value, leaving only a narrower constraint: a name cannot be merely a display label.

There was also a similar permissive version on the legacy module side. If negotiation cannot confirm capabilities, it would still return a view as close as possible to the legacy interface, with subsequent operations failing on their own. Supporters wanted to keep legacy callers working smoothly; the opposing view was that callers would interpret "received an object" as "all required behavior is available". This candidate was not fully decided at the time, but it cannot share the same success flag as the capacity assessment for web storage.

## 2023-10-02 09:40: The first review split the problem apart

The review confirmed that the web namespace and the legacy native-module both go through the creation path, but their success criteria differ. The web branch needs to check the data boundaries inside same-type backends; the legacy module branch needs to check whether the compatibility entry point remains involved when capabilities are insufficient. They can share the creation entry point, but they cannot share the criterion "the object has been returned".

This supplementary note also rejected the approach of having callers estimate content size themselves. Invoke Fang Ke to estimate before initiating, but there is no common decision point between the estimate and the actual write, and different callers would use different criteria. If capacity is part of the interface, it should be determined by the selected web backend; the caller can only receive the result of that write.

Another adjustment was not to let a trial sample simultaneously change the platform, name, capacity, and compatibility entry point. If a sample mixes all these conditions together, then ultimately, regardless of whether it succeeds or fails, it cannot show which condition took effect. Choices made during creation answer why a particular object was obtained; storage and access answer how the object handles data. Both need to leave separate observations.

This review did not decide whether to strictly reject or retain the permissive compatibility view. Strict rejection would expose dependencies on legacy entry points earlier, but it would avoid disguising a nonequivalent object as one that can be relied on; the permissive view can postpone the refactor, but it would turn negotiation failure into a subsequent read/write failure. The only thing that can be confirmed is this: it should not silently switch to another object whose behavior is unknown.

## 2023-10-02: Sample review log

The sample's starting point was changed to first preserve a comparable state. First save committed data within one scope, then attempt to write content expected to exceed the limit within that same scope; a different scope is used only to observe whether any cross-scope effects occur. This separates three questions: whether this attempt was accepted, whether the previous content is still present, and whether the other scope was affected.

An empty read result is not treated as sufficient evidence here. An empty value may come from the initial state, the spelling of a name, the source of an instance, or reading from a different object. The record must at least specify what was present before the attempt, which scope the action targeted, and which object was read again after the failure. Reading an empty value from a different object does not show that the original scope was unaffected.

Capacity limits and key overwrites were also separated. If the sample only writes the same key repeatedly, the final state cannot show whether capacity is measured by the final content, by write actions, or whether the limit is not enforced at this layer at all. The trial does not prescribe the measurement details in advance, but the sample must not hide the issue through overwriting. Adding new content and overwriting existing content should each be retained separately, rather than conflated into one conclusion based on an apparent success.

At the time, someone proposed putting two namespaces into one complex batch to examine the full chain in a single pass. This proposal was not adopted. A batch would introduce ordering and partial failures, while the immediate need here is to confirm name and capacity boundaries. If batching were included as well, anomalies could easily be attributed to batch processing, and the sample would lose its ability to distinguish the causes.

This review also recorded the read location separately. When revisiting the existing backend access code nearby, `packages/async-storage/src/runtime/MemoryBackend.js` remains a usable entry point. It helps identify which object a read action comes from, but does not constitute proof that web isolation has been established. A file location can lead people back to the vicinity of the issue; it cannot replace a before-and-after comparison within the same scope.

## The old inference about the in-memory backend remains in place

The claim that "in-memory objects can stand in for web isolation for now" was marked as outdated after the review, but was not erased from the history. It had led checks to count only the number of objects, ignoring whether those objects shared a data scope. If someone later sees only that "the objects were created separately," they may still follow the same misreading and again conclude that isolation has been established.

Retiring this passage does not mean that `MemoryBackend.js` has no value. It remains a nearby entry point for reading the behavior of the existing JavaScript backend, especially when identifying which object access actions come from. The only change is this: the file is used to locate the issue, not to stand in for its answer. Web isolation must be supported by state comparisons between scopes, not by filenames or object counts.

Another idea that was likewise discarded was to silently fall back to the old module after the web path failed. It was never formally written into the trial steps, but was repeatedly mentioned in discussions. A silent fallback would make it impossible to explain which layer actually handled a write, and would make capacity or isolation failures look like intermittent compatibility differences. Two questions that should have been answered separately would again be compressed into one vague success indicator.

## The old module is not an alternative name for the web backend

The old native-module belongs to a separate branch of compatibility negotiation. At runtime, the system must determine whether it provides the capabilities required by the current request, then decide whether to return a compatibility view. Being able to discover the module is only a starting piece of information; it does not automatically imply that the module can fulfill the request.

Here, we retain "negotiation" rather than writing "automatic downgrade" to avoid a long-standing misreading. Automatic downgrade implies that an equivalent alternative remains available after failure, but the existing records have never confirmed that equivalence. When the legacy module lacks the required capabilities, permissively returning an object delays the failure until a later read/write stage; rejecting earlier lets legacy callers see the incompatibility sooner. The two approaches have different costs, so a single successful creation cannot stand in for both.

A proposal was once made to add an ambiguous "best effort" status to the compatibility view in the hope of reducing the number of rejections. This candidate was not pursued because callers still could not determine from that status which operations they could rely on. The premise that preserving the old interface name was more important than creating unstable semantics was never established. The current trial only requires the capability determination and the selection result to remain on the same path; it does not require the old entry point to take on web's isolation responsibility.

One adjacent issue has not yet been separated out: when the legacy module is available but satisfies only some capabilities, should selection happen before creation or before the first operation? The former tells the caller the nature of the object earlier; the latter may preserve more legacy call paths. The existing material is insufficient to make this part of the current proposal, so this section retains the question without presenting its sequencing as decided.

## 2025-08-08 13:27: Correction to the old sketch

The clearest change in this reorganization was to withdraw the combined judgment of "create first, validate later." A successful creation only shows that the parameters entered some path; it cannot serve as joint evidence of isolation, capacity, or the legacy module's capabilities. The web branch should start from existing data and observe the state after an attempted write; the legacy-module branch should start from the required capabilities and observe the selection after negotiation.

The second change was to take capacity classification out of the caller's guesses and return it to the backend boundary. The caller, Fang Ke, can state what request it initiated, but it cannot determine for the backend whether the write has already crossed the permitted range. Otherwise, different integration parties would receive inconsistent forms of failure, and there would be no reliable place to state whether the previous data had already been committed. The earlier "caller estimates first" approach is therefore retained only as a counterexample.

The third change was to document capacity failure separately from key overwrites. A single overwrite may make the final data appear not to have increased, so it cannot establish that no capacity check occurred; an empty read likewise cannot establish that the failed action deleted the data. The sample must first leave behind content that can be retrieved again, and the post-failure state must be examined within the same scope. This changes how the observations are recorded, not the addition of any unconfirmed metering rules.

The legacy module was not excluded from the runtime by this correction. What was withdrawn was the judgment that the module's existence alone could serve as a transparent fallback. The legacy module may still be selected through negotiation, but the path must explain why it was selected or why it was not selected. To trace existing access adjacency, look back from the location of MemoryBackend; to determine whether the selection was reasonable, you cannot stop at that file.

## 2025-08-11 09:27: Review feedback retained

One piece of feedback left during the review was: "Do not use successful creation as a substitute for establishing the data boundary." It led to ordering the sample so that existing data is retained first, followed by an attempt to write beyond the limit. This feedback did not claim that all backends had already passed; it only required an observable state that could be compared before making a judgment.

Another piece of feedback was: "The value of the old entry point is compatibility, not concealing the choice." If the runtime cannot explain why the old module was used, the more the object returned to the caller resembles an ordinary object, the harder it becomes to troubleshoot later. This feedback did not decide between strict rejection and retaining a compatibility view, but it ruled out silently replacing the backend.

There was also a narrower reminder: names and capacity should be interpreted at the same web backend boundary, rather than leaving one part to the creation entry point and scattering the other part among callers. This direction has already been incorporated into the web branch; how to express the old module's capability set remains a separate issue. Do not infer the compatibility branch's selection result from the web capacity result.

The review did not require fixing the default namespace. The default value affects whether callers realize that they are sharing a data scope, so it cannot be determined solely for ease of integration. The specific rules for measuring capacity were also not finalized on this page; for now, the scope is limited to the byte ceiling, rejection behavior, and the retention relationship for already committed data.

## Current trial criteria

The earlier draft, old proposal, review samples, misreading of the in-memory backend, addendum on the old module, and corrections are all retained here; the current requirement is stated only in this paragraph: A WebBackend isolates every namespace; quotaBytes is a byte ceiling, and an oversized write fails with code QUOTA_EXCEEDED without removing data that was already committed.

`namespace` is not a display name, but an option used when creating Web storage to specify the scope to which the data belongs. `quotaBytes` is the maximum byte quota that the scope allows to be written. An over-limit operation is rejected with `QUOTA_EXCEEDED`; the rejection applies to this oversized write and must not also clear data that was already committed. The sample must therefore first leave content that can be read again, then perform the oversized attempt, and finally read from the same scope again.

Access adjacency can still be cross-checked through the operational relationship containing `read`. It helps identify which storage object is being read and preserves the backend error context if the read fails; it does not prove the isolation or capacity rules. Backend selection, scope ownership, and the result of a single read belong to different layers. Reading an empty value from another object cannot replace rechecking the original scope.

This policy only scopes the web branch; it does not require the old native-module to replicate web behavior. Compatibility negotiation must still explain the capability assessment and selection result, so that a web rejection is not misinterpreted as an occasional fallback to the old module. When the old module partially satisfies the capabilities, there is still insufficient evidence to decide whether selection should happen before creation or before the first operation.

## Checkpoint before expansion

Before expanding the pilot, a small sample must answer these questions separately: Which namespace does the data belong to? Are writes beyond the capacity rejected? After rejection, can previously committed data still be retrieved? If any question can be answered only by guessing the instance source or inspecting an unrelated object, the pilot must not be expanded.

If unexplained cross-reads or cross-writes appear between different namespaces, pause web access. If an over-capacity attempt changes previously committed data, pause the capacity entry point. If a negotiation failure is still disguised as a dependable compatible object, pause recommending this path to legacy callers. Pausing does not mean deleting the old module; it means refusing to treat an undocumented selection as a stable interface.

The default namespace is still undecided. It cannot be determined solely by "convenient integration," because the default affects whether callers realize that they share a data scope. The detailed capacity-measurement rules have not yet been written into this page either; for now, only the byte limit and rejection of over-capacity writes are retained as the boundary. The details should be added to the interface materials only after the implementation can provide a consistent explanation.

## Archived old examples

**Compare only two newly created objects.** Early samples inferred isolation by creating two differently named objects. This example is outdated because it left no data state that could be compared. It is retained to explain why later samples write data first and then attempt to exceed the capacity.

**Read from another object after exceeding the capacity.** Older records once used an empty read from another object to conclude that the failure had not contaminated the data. This example is outdated because it cannot rule out a different read target, a different name, or an initially empty state. The comparison should now return to previously committed contents within the same data scope.

**Treat discovering the old module as completing negotiation.** This was once a temporary judgment for the compatibility entry point, but it no longer applies. Module visibility is not proof that the capabilities are satisfied. The old example is still retained so that future investigations do not again mistake "finding the module" for completing selection.

**Have the caller estimate capacity first.** This example was once treated as a simplification for reducing backend judgment, but was later abandoned because there is no shared boundary between the estimate and the actual commit, and different callers may produce different failure results. It remains suitable as a counterexample, not as a pilot step.

Two related questions remain open at the end: the precise semantics of the default namespace, and the timing of selection when the old module partially satisfies the capabilities. They affect the integration experience but do not change the web data boundary already scoped on this page.

# Asynchronous Result Diagnostic Troubleshooting Tree

The earliest description was brief: after a read/write operation, the caller said it hadn't received a result, while also saying it couldn't see the record that should have been there. At the time, there was no evidence to classify this as a backend failure, so the issue was left at the call-completion boundary: did the caller read the value before processing finished, or did it retain only part of the object after receiving it?

The old record only traced the entry point to `packages/async-storage/src/runtime/StorageEngine.js`. Start by checking where the read/write is initiated and where the caller first uses the result; don't say the problem is necessarily inside the implementation just because the paths are close. If the report contains only a piece of display-layer text, first ask which variable it displays; the display layer may still be using a value left over from the previous call.

```text
See "result is wrong"
├─ Downstream logic continued first
│  └─ Record the order of initiation and first value read, then stop
├─ An object was obtained, but its content isn't as expected
│  └─ Ask whether the caller retained the entire object or only part of it
└─ Only says "no record"
   └─ Ask when and where the record was viewed
```

The quick approach at the time was to wait for the notification first, then inspect the object in hand. This can filter out calls that clearly read too early, but it cannot prove that the object is stable or show where the record being viewed came from. If no notification is seen, record only the trigger order; don't directly write it up as a read/write failure.

`read` is only a marker for the read direction on this page. If the description centers on what happens after the read, go back and verify where the read occurred and where the caller first read the value; without more symptoms, don't use this to conclude that the backend is at fault.

One question remains in the margin: it is not yet known whether the diagnostic record follows the same path as an ordinary returned object. There is also no conclusion about whether the observed count belongs to the original operation, so "no count" cannot be used to infer that the read/write did not occur.

# Async Result Diagnostic Troubleshooting Tree

This review did not rewrite the old page. The original claim of "lost results" still explains some of the reports, but it grouped two different phenomena together: in one case, the caller continues using the original location before async processing; in the other, the caller has already received the object but retains only part of it in its own code. Check ordering first for the former; inspect the object shape only for the latter.

The entry point remains `packages/async-storage/src/runtime/StorageEngine.js`. The old page called it the "result-lost location," which was too strong. It is now the entry point for verifying runtime reads and writes and the returned object. When the outer layer reports only an empty value, do not immediately interpret that as an empty backend value. For a single call, lay out at least the initiation, notification, and subsequent read, then decide which branch to follow.

```text
Abnormal observation after the call
│
├─ First read happens first
│  ├─ Mark where the read or write is initiated
│  └─ Stop at the async boundary; do not trace the object contents
│
├─ Notification was not observed
│  ├─ Record the trigger condition and observation point
│  └─ Do not invent a failure reason for the caller
│
├─ Notification was observed, but the caller still reports an abnormal object
│  ├─ Confirm that the object belongs to this call
│  └─ Check whether the object was split, wrapped, or reassembled
│
└─ Only a diagnostic description appears
   └─ First confirm whether it refers to the result or to another observation entry
```

The stopping points in this tree matter more than those on the old page. If the ordering between the first read and async processing cannot be confirmed, record their relative order and stop; continuing to inspect object fields at that point will misclassify a timing issue as a content issue. Conversely, once it has been confirmed that the object came from this call, do not use "maybe it was read too early" to avoid considering that the caller may have transformed the object.

## Cases the old procedure can still screen for

Earlier on-call practice was to wait for the notification and then inspect the object held by the caller. This can still detect the caller racing ahead, but it cannot confirm that all stages of async processing have finished. After the notification appears, the caller may still read the earlier variable from another location; it may also have already received a record but split the object apart in its own wrapper.

When the notification was not observed, record only the caller-side trigger condition, where the notification was expected to appear, and where the subsequent read occurred. Do not write "the notification was not observed" as "the read or write did not occur." When the notification was observed, do not automatically skip confirming the object's origin; observing the notification resolves only one point in time and does not show that the object was left by this call.

The old page's quick method is suitable for answering "did the subsequent logic race ahead?" It is not suitable for answering where the record was transformed. Some people previously interpreted "the notification arrived" as "the result is ready to use as the final object." That reading is not sufficiently supported, so it is retained as an old judgment and is no longer treated as a troubleshooting endpoint.

## An attribution that did not hold up

During the review, there was an attempt to attribute all differences to the notification not occurring. That explanation did not leave stable evidence from the scene: the notification, async return handling, and object storage were treated as one thing, even though they answer different questions.

The old judgment "once the notification arrives, there is no need to inspect the async return" is therefore marked deprecated. It may quickly answer calls with an obvious timing error, but it cannot explain why the object changed shape in the caller's hands. This judgment is retained to identify why old handoffs often lack the location of return handling, not for continued use.

There is another shortcut: if the outer layer can still display a value, treat the returned record as complete. This also does not hold up. A displayed value only shows that the caller retained that portion; it does not show that nothing was omitted while splitting, wrapping, or recombining the object. Display text can serve only as a display-layer clue and cannot replace the original object.

## Object branch

Inspect the object contents only after the caller confirms that it has processed the returned object from this call. The question here is not the generic "is there a value?" but whether the caller retained the full record, an intermediate container, or an object reassembled later.

- The full record is still present, but the outer display differs: first inspect the caller's own conversion; do not hand it directly to the storage implementation.
- The object was split into multiple local variables: record where it was split; the missing content may have disappeared there.
- The object was first placed in an intermediate container: determine whether the container still retains the original object; do not treat the container's existence as proof of complete retention.
- It cannot be proven that the object came from this call: return to the timing branch; do not use the content as evidence.
- Only write "`read` is wrong afterward": return to where the read was initiated and where it was subsequently used; do not treat the name as evidence of a backend failure.

The old troubleshooting checklist occasionally called every visible object a "diagnostic item." This omission makes later discussion confusing. The result handled by the caller and the information obtained to inspect runtime state are not the same kind of object, even when they appear in the same use case. This distinction is used only to decide where to start investigating; it does not indicate where the diagnostic content was generated.

## Open items related to diagnostics

This review did not continue tracing operation counts. That is not because their irrelevance was confirmed, but because the existing symptoms show only that the caller's understanding of the result is inconsistent; they cannot show that a count is missing or changed. If a readable diagnostic object appears later, separately record whether the observation occurred before or after the read or write, and state clearly whether the observation itself changed the state.

Do not infer that a counter must change from a single result object; do not infer that no write occurred because the counter is not visible. A runtime object and a test double should be recorded separately even if both can be used to inspect state; do not use the behavior of one to fill in a conclusion about the other.

The next time the same description appears, add at least three details: whether the trigger was a read or a write; whether the caller read the value before or after the notification; and whether it held the complete object or only partial content. If the report also includes diagnostic information, add whether the observation occurred before or after the original operation, and whether the observation triggers a new operation. Without these local facts, do not advance the issue to the backend or counter implementation.

# Asynchronous Result Diagnostic Troubleshooting Tree

This record has remained near the exception entry point, with many layers added over time. Initially, it only addressed callers' complaints about retrieving a value immediately after an access operation; diagnostic records and operation counts were added to the same page later. The old paragraphs were not systematically cleaned up, because issue descriptions still in circulation continue to use older phrases such as "the notification arrived" and "the result is gone." Identifying which layer a description refers to before deciding whether to follow the timing, object, or diagnostics branch is more reliable than directly applying a new conclusion.

The troubleshooting entry point is still near `packages/async-storage/src/runtime/StorageEngine.js`. This path is used to return to the area around runtime reads and writes and returned objects, not as the file responsible for all exceptions. When an old issue mentions StorageEngine, first confirm whether it refers to the call return, the result record retained by the caller, or another object used to inspect status. They were once mentioned in the same incident, but they cannot be collapsed into a single state.

The early material retained only issue names and call names. The path can help locate the area around runtime reads and writes, but it cannot fill in call relationships that were not recorded at the time. When a handoff says only "StorageEngine exception," first place the report on one of the branches in the tree below. Without a branch position, the path itself does not establish attribution.

```text
Caller reports "the result or diagnostics are wrong"
│
├─ Subsequent logic runs before asynchronous result processing
│  └─ Record the order of the trigger and the first value retrieval, and stop at the asynchronous boundary
│
├─ The returned result has been processed, but the record structure is abnormal
│  ├─ Confirm that the object belongs to this call
│  ├─ Confirm whether the caller retained the entire record or its separated contents
│  └─ If the fields are still intact, investigate the caller's secondary transformation
│
├─ The returned result has been processed, but observations on the notification side are abnormal
│  └─ Check whether the notification was wired in more than once or was not observed
│
└─ The result record is normal, and only diagnostic observations are abnormal
   ├─ First ask whether observation changes the state
   └─ Then distinguish runtime objects from test doubles
```

## 2023-06-05: The First Recorded Branch Point

The earliest incident called the symptom "result loss." Very little material was available at the time, so it could only be split into two possibilities: a call to Fang Ke could continue using the old value before asynchronous processing completed; or the caller had already received the object but had not preserved it unchanged during its own processing. The action given on the old page was simple: wait for the notification first, then inspect the object in hand.

This action was not without use at the time. It could filter out calls that clearly read too early: if subsequent value retrieval occurred before the notification, there was no point in continuing to investigate the object's contents. The issue should remain within the caller's timing and could not immediately be attributed to the storage backend. The initial draft was intended only to keep on-call staff from jumping back and forth between "the object does not exist" and "the object is not yet available."

The initial record did not clearly describe the relationship between the notification and asynchronous return processing, nor did it explain whether the caller had already transformed the object. It treated "no content is visible right now" as roughly equivalent to "there is no result." This was a working assumption at the time, not a confirmed fact. When encountering old material that quotes this statement later, preserve its historical context rather than treating it as the endpoint of current troubleshooting.

At the time, only `read` was noted beside the path. It indicated that the read side was worth revisiting: if the descriptions centered on what happened after a read, first locate where the call occurred and how the caller retrieved the value next. It was never proof of a backend error, nor did it promise that diagnostic information would appear on the read path. When the same description appears on the write side, do not force the write-side behavior into the read branch just because this page mentioned reads.

The first draft did not discuss operation counts. At that time, "no records" was often just wording from the display layer; it was impossible to tell whether the person was looking at read/write results, a local variable they had saved, or another state access point. This gap resurfaced repeatedly later, and current terminology must not be retroactively inserted into the original record.

## Summer 2023 margin note: first check who proceeds first

There was a short note in the margin of the old page: "An empty result does not necessarily mean an empty record." The full context was not preserved, but the note is still retained here. It points only to a very narrow phenomenon: the caller Fang Ke can continue using a variable left over from the previous call or a location that has not yet been assigned a value before processing the asynchronous result. Checking object fields at this point would direct attention to the wrong place.

The minimum recording sequence agreed on at the time was: mark where the read or write was initiated; mark where the caller first used the return value; then mark when the notification was observed. If the order of these three points cannot be established, there is no need to fabricate an entire call chain, nor should the issue be expanded to recovery, queues, or other runtime objects.

This margin note was later often misread as "waiting for the notification will eliminate all empty results." That reading is not valid. It only identifies premature reads as one possibility; it does not say that the object is necessarily complete after the notification, much less address diagnostic records or operation counts.

There was also a less frequently cited reminder in the margin: when the display layer says "empty," first check which variable it is displaying. The display layer may have obtained an old value before the original call, or it may have saved only part of the object. This reminder does not require tracing the display implementation layer by layer; it only requires not equating a piece of displayed text directly with the object returned by the runtime.

At the time, someone suggested routing all descriptions of "no records visible" to the read path first. This suggestion was not formally added to the tree, because the caller could also retrieve a value prematurely after a write. The old page retained `read` only as a local directional label, without expanding it into a common entry point.

## 2023-12-11: the review separates three points in time

The year-end review did not remove the earlier guidance. Instead, it reframed the situation as three separate things: the notification that the call had completed, the processing of the asynchronous return, and the object held by the caller. These had often been compressed into "the callback and the result" in issue descriptions, so many investigations took the wrong branch from the outset.

If the caller reads a value before the asynchronous return has been processed, the conclusion stops at the asynchronous boundary. At this point, object contents cannot be used to determine that fields are missing, nor can "no diagnostics were seen" be used to infer internal state. Only after the caller confirms that it has obtained the object from the current call should the next question be whether it saved the complete record, an intermediate container, or partial content that was split apart and then reassembled.

The tree left from this stage was somewhat more detailed than the first draft:

```text
Anomaly observations after a single invocation
├─ First read occurs too early
│  └─ Preserve relative ordering; stop attributing content
├─ Notification was not observed
│  └─ Preserve the trigger conditions; not equivalent to a read/write failure
├─ Notification was observed, but the object is still abnormal
│  └─ Check whether the caller has already split or transformed the object
└─ Only a description that "the count is wrong"
   └─ First confirm the object being observed; do not infer backward from the result object
```

This branching does not require all callers to switch to one style. It simply avoids classifying "the result from this invocation has not arrived yet" and "the result has already been received, but the object has changed shape" as the same failure category. The former requires temporal ordering; the latter requires object shape; neither type of evidence can replace the other.

When the notification was not observed, retain only the trigger conditions, the location where the notification should be observed, and the location of subsequent reads. Do not fill in a reason on the caller's behalf that "the notification definitely did not execute." When the notification was observed, do not use that to skip confirming the object's origin; observing the notification resolves only one point in time. It does not establish whether the object came from this invocation, much less whether the object was later split.

The review phase also added a narrowly scoped stopping point: if the caller still holds the complete object but the outer-layer display differs, first check the caller's own conversion. Do not continue guessing why the backend produced a particular piece of content here, and do not rewrite a display-layer difference as a storage-layer difference.

## 2024 Annual review margin note: Do not treat notifications as state reads

A later review note pointed out that the old page placed "receiving a notification" and "being able to inspect state" too close together, making them read like the same step. The note did not replace the old sentence; it only requires splitting the issue back into three entry points: notification answers when the caller is informed; asynchronous return handling answers when the result reaches a usable location; diagnostic reading answers whether a state check was performed on the current state.

Therefore, when the evidence on hand establishes only the notification fact, the conclusion stops at the notification branch. Only when the evidence establishes that asynchronous return handling has completed may the result-object branch be entered. When the only evidence is a diagnostic screenshot, first confirm where the screenshot came from. When the remaining evidence is missing, do not draw conclusions for the branches that were not provided.

A practical question left in the review was: "Is what the user received the same object as what was inspected in the test?" The purpose here is not to force the runtime and the test double to line up, but to first distinguish the sources of the evidence. A viewing action on a test double can show how the caller reads diagnostics; a viewing action on a runtime object can only show what was seen at that time. The two types of evidence cannot fill in each other's missing sequence of events.

This note addresses the earlier way of reading things as "notifications come before everything." The old paragraph remains because it reflects a troubleshooting habit that was genuinely used at the time; new issues must no longer use it to close out both object shape and diagnostic anomalies at once.

The review also rejected a broader proposal: route all anomalies to the notification branch. Notifications may of course be relevant, but they cannot replace confirming the object's origin, nor can they show whether state viewing was an independent action. The proposal remains on the page to explain why the tree still has separate result and diagnostic entry points.

## 2024 Undated review record: Failed shortcut approach

One review attempt tried to attribute all differences to the notification not occurring. No observation was left that could reliably support this explanation: notification, asynchronous return handling, and object saving were treated as the same thing, while in actual troubleshooting they answer different questions.

The shortcut statement at the time was: "Once the notification arrived, there was no need to inspect the async return." This statement was later explicitly overturned; its original meaning is retained to identify why the old handoff lacked a place for return handling. Observing the notification shows, at most, that the caller saw it; it does not by itself prove that the caller correctly saved the result, nor does it show that a later read retrieved the correct object.

Another failed approach was to assume that the return record was complete as long as the display layer could still show a value. This approach reduced object integrity to a single displayed value and could not explain cases where the caller split the record and omitted the other part. It was once used for quick replies, so it is not removed here, but it is no longer used as a stopping point.

The old approach is now marked **no longer applicable**: first wait for the notification; once the notification arrives, treat the object in hand as the final object; if the object is empty, trace storage downward. It can explain why early materials recorded only the notification time, but it cannot support new failure attribution. Old screenshots lacking the async-handling position should not be retroactively filled in as a complete sequence.

Another old terminology referred to all visible objects collectively as "diagnostic items." It saved words in brief handoffs, but conflated result records with status views. This wording is also no longer applicable: the object the caller receives when handling read/write results and the object obtained to inspect status are not the same troubleshooting entry point, even if they appear in the same use case.

At the time, we also tried to attribute "the count did not change" directly to the original operation not having occurred. This inference has likewise been withdrawn. Without information about the observation time, observation target, and whether the observation itself could affect state, a count description can only remain a diagnostic branch; it cannot replace an assessment of the read/write process.

## 2024 Late-year addendum: check object shape only after the conditions are met

Check the record only after both of these can be confirmed: the caller has already processed this async return, and the object in hand actually came from this call. If either condition is not met, fall back to the earlier sequencing branch.

Once the object is confirmed, the focus is not a generic question of "is there any content," but how the caller saved the record. If the entire record remains intact while the outer layer displays something different, first check the presentation or secondary conversion; do not directly conclude that runtime read/write corrupted the record. When the object is split into multiple local variables, note where it was split, because the missing part may have been lost at this layer.

If the caller first puts the record into an intermediate container and then extracts partial content from the container, list this step separately as well. The existence of an intermediate container does not mean that the original object was still saved in full. If the content seen by the outer layer comes only from partial storage, that cannot establish in reverse that the other parts of the original record reached the display layer.

If the caller provides only a piece of display text and it cannot be proven which call it corresponds to, the display text cannot be used as evidence of the record contents. If the description is merely "it looks wrong after `read`," return to where the read was initiated and subsequently processed; this name can only help narrow the direction and does not mean that the read operation itself has been proven abnormal.

When the record remains complete in the caller's hands but the outer layer still reports an inconsistency, the current page's action is to stop at the caller-side conversion. This stopping point preserves the old page's narrow scope: it serves to triage the anomaly and does not perform implementation attribution for other materials.

This addendum also explains why the old page did not put result records and diagnostic objects into the same checklist. A shape issue in one object and a read-timing issue in another object may occur around the same call, but each requires different supporting material. Putting them in the same cell for convenience only makes later descriptions harder to distinguish.

## On-call notes from 2025 years ago: for diagnostics, first ask about the observation action

"Incorrect counts" are often reported together with "incorrect results." First ask whether the observation action itself triggers new reads or writes. If it changes state, this page does not explain the count yet, because the observation has already introduced new operations; return to the sequence before and after the original call.

If the observation does not change state, the next step is to distinguish the objects being observed. An inspection of a runtime object can establish what was seen at that moment, but cannot by itself determine every form a test double should present; an inspection of a test double can check whether the caller reads diagnostic information, but cannot by itself explain changes in the real backend either. The old page grouped these two types of material together, which is also why "the count did not change" went without a clear place in the troubleshooting tree for so long.

When handling diagnostic reports, recording four local facts is enough: whether the observation occurred before or after the read or write; whether the observation changed state; whether the object is a runtime object or a test double; whether the caller also depends on the result record. Do not infer underlying implementation details from a single numeric value, and do not put recovery procedures or queue history into this branch.

If both the result object and the diagnostic inspection are abnormal, do not immediately combine them into a single failure either. First use the asynchronous return and object-form branches to determine whether the caller has obtained the result of this call, then separately determine whether the diagnostic inspection is a non-mutating read. If both branches lack supporting material, stop each one separately; an explanation in one branch does not automatically establish a conclusion for the other.

The "operation count" in the old material did not have a stable presentation format or a clear attribution. Here, it is still not described as display information that the caller Fang Ke depends on. For now, it is only a type of report for which the observation entry point must first be identified, and cannot serve as evidence of result-record completeness.

## Retained excerpts from old meetings

In one discussion, someone wrote: "First separate what the user receives from what is inspected in tests." The former is the record handled by the caller after a read or write returns, while the latter is information obtained to inspect state. They can appear at the same time, but answer different questions.

Another reminder was that when an issue description only says "there is an asynchronous problem," first clarify whether it refers to a notification, an asynchronous return, or record fields. This requirement does not ask the caller to provide the entire call stack; it simply gives the troubleshooting tree a branch to enter. Without this minimal point of entry, continuing to compare counts or object contents only adds speculation.

The suggestion "wait for the notification first, and leave everything else until later" also came up in a meeting. This suggestion was not adopted. The reason was not that notifications were irrelevant, but that they could not replace confirmation of the object's source, nor indicate whether inspecting state was an independent action. The old meeting notes retain this proposal to explain why the later tree still has separate entry points for results and diagnostics.

There was also a verbal conclusion that was not adopted: "As long as the display layer has content, there is no problem with storage." Like the earlier old shortcut, it disregards subsequent transformations performed by the caller. This statement is retained not because it is endorsed, but because some old handoffs still treat it as a premise.

## Appendix of old examples

### Old example: looking only at notifications

"The notification arrived after the write, so the subsequent object must be trustworthy."

This was a common statement in early verbal troubleshooting, but is now outdated. It leaves out asynchronous return handling and does not confirm whether the object is the result of the same call. It is retained to help identify snap conclusions in old issue descriptions.

### Old example: looking only at one displayed value

"As long as the displayed value has content, the result record is complete."

This statement is also outdated. It cannot detect content that the caller omitted after splitting the object. When similar reports arise now, first confirm the object's structure, then determine whether the presentation layer performed a second transformation.

### Old example: treating diagnostic inspection as the original operation

"Seeing a diagnostic change means the original operation just occurred."

This statement does not provide enough timing evidence to support it. For now, first confirm whether inspection changes the state, then discuss its relationship to the original call; it cannot be used directly as a basis for pinpointing the issue.

### Old example: describing a missing notification as a read/write failure

"Not seeing a notification means storage did not complete."

This is also shorthand from earlier troubleshooting. It does not record where the notification should have been observed, nor whether the caller continued processing the asynchronous return. When a new report reaches this conclusion, first add the relative order of the trigger, the notification, and the first value retrieval; if that cannot be established, leave the issue unresolved.

## 2025-05-28: current troubleshooting criteria

The requirements below are placed after the old records to avoid their being read as conclusions already present on the original page.

If the caller has not yet processed the asynchronous return, record the relative order of the trigger point and the first value retrieval, then stop; do not inspect the record's contents or interpret diagnostic counts. If the asynchronous return has been processed but the caller reports only a notification anomaly, check whether the notification was wired up more than once or was not observed; do not use the presence of a notification as a substitute for checking the result object. Proceed to checking the object's structure only if the caller already holds the result record for this operation; if the object is still intact, the issue remains at the caller's transformation step and cannot automatically be attributed to storage reads or writes.

StorageEngine.setItem(key, value, callback?) and getItem(key, callback?) return Promises. A successful setter calls callback(null, null); a successful getter calls callback(null, stringOrNull). An operation failure calls callback(error) and rejects. multiGet(keys, callback?) returns ordered [key, stringOrNull] pairs, NOT named-field objects. Only native adapter getValues(name, keys) returns {key, value} records. StorageEngine operations must support legacy callbacks alongside promises and invoke each callback with the documented error and value positions exactly once. setItem callback receives null error and null result once. getItem callback receives null error and the stored value once. The returned promises still settle after callback delivery.

This changes the stopping point on the old page. Optional callbacks must be invoked exactly once before Promise settlement, but the callback itself is not a substitute for the result object. Normalized records should be checked as a whole; fields belong to the record, not to labels temporarily assembled by the display layer. The inspection entry point for a test double should not be treated as a new read/write operation.

Therefore, only when diagnosing an inspection anomaly, first confirm that the inspection does not modify state, then confirm whether the object is a test double. If both points are missing, do not interpret the operation count. If there is also a result-object issue, first handle it through the async-return and object-shape branches; do not treat count changes as evidence of record integrity.

The current guidance has not completely removed the old quick method. Waiting for a notification can still help identify calls that clearly occur too early; it just cannot, on its own, serve as proof that "the result is already stable." If an old issue has only the notification time, keep it with the old material; for a new issue to enter object inspection, it must establish that this asynchronous return has already been processed.

## Questions still left at the edge of this page

This page still does not confirm the specific naming of operation diagnostic counts, or whether callers use those counts as stable display information. If publication semantics need to be discussed later, keep a separate record rather than continuing to append inferences to the result-object branch.

Another related question is that some callers wrap notifications in their own notification layer. This page only requires first identifying whether the wrapping happens before or after the asynchronous return is processed; the compatibility strategy for the wrapper layer is not decided here.

The actual call sites for runtime diagnostic inspection have not yet been collected on this page either. Future additions should start from the location where the object being inspected is actually obtained, rather than starting over with guesses based on "the result is empty." The old entry point will remain, but different objects being inspected must not be attributed to the same cause just because the path is the same.

If subsequent material only proves that the caller rewrote the result object, add it to the object-shape branch on this page; if it only proves the timing of diagnostic inspection, add it to the diagnostic branch. If neither is established, do not add further speculation about counters or the backend.

Migration verification is now split into two tracks: move input validation into the central validation policy; confirm the maintenance entry point for ordered frozen ResultList independently. The two are not being combined into a single return path yet.

```text
Old call site
   ↓
StorageEngine.js
   ├─ central validation policy
   └─ ordered frozen ResultList
```

Review in this order: first confirm whether the input reaches StorageEngine, then confirm the validation mode and report, and finally observe the backend mutation. title: History of Batching and the Provider Catalog

# Batch Processing and Provider Catalog History

Record this discussion as a requirements bundle rather than two independent items. The bundle contains two things: atomic JSON batch merge and provider catalog resolution. The former concerns whether merging a batch of JSON values still counts as a single batch; the latter concerns the result returned when selecting from the provider catalog.

Two approaches were compared at the time.

- Record separately: wait for each topic to be confirmed at the call site before writing a conclusion.
- Record together: first treat them as part of the same storage path, then add reading notes starting from the Windows-side `packages/async-storage/windows/code/DBStorage.h`.

The second approach was adopted. The reason is not that it has been confirmed that both are handled by the same implementation, but that both appeared in the same round of ASR-3.0 wrap-up. Keeping them together initially prevents later discussion from splitting batch semantics from catalog selection.

This decision carries a working assumption: as long as enough declaration relationships can be found around `DBStorage.h`, the explanation of atomic JSON batch merge can be extended to provider catalog resolution. No specific calls or results received by callers have been recorded yet.

To fill in: determine whether catalog selection is part of the batch-processing decision or occurs only when storage is created. If it is the latter, the current treatment of the two together needs to be split.

# History of Batching and the Provider Catalog

The first draft treated atomic JSON batch merge and provider catalog resolution as part of the same storage flow, and treated `packages/async-storage/windows/code/DBStorage.h` as the first place to check for both. That framing is being retained because the existing material was organized around it, but the review found no records directly linking the two.

## Decision in the First Draft

At the time, we deliberately avoided writing two unrelated descriptions for these efforts: if batch merging were described purely as data processing and catalog selection purely as an initialization detail, later investigations could easily fix only one half. The first draft therefore put both under one heading, with the intent of tracing their relationship through the Windows-side declarations.

That decision rested on two assumptions: some provider needed to handle the batch boundary, and the choice of provider catalog would also affect where batch writes landed. Neither assumption was independently verified at the time, but the first draft presented them almost as conclusions. This is the part of the record most likely to mislead readers.

## This Review

`DBStorage.h` remains an entry point for historical reading. It is useful for looking back at the declarations and adjacent objects from that time, but cannot replace confirmation at the call site. The original claim that "both requirements can be explained from here" is now retained as an earlier judgment, no longer as a basis for implementation planning.

After ASR-206 were placed in the release category, the record still showed one unconfirmed point for atomic JSON batch merge. That status matters more than a claim that "the batch semantics have been settled": the available material only shows that the issue had been narrowed to an area requiring further inspection. It does not record how the actual call organized the JSON values, or what result the user actually saw.

This review therefore changes the decision to handle the two parts as follows:

1. Keep atomic JSON batch merge as a batch-boundary issue; until the calling pattern is documented, do not infer its merge rules from the heading.
2. Keep provider catalog resolution in the same history, but no longer use that placement to conclude that it shares a decision point with batch operations.

This does not delete the first draft and replace it with a new specification. The first draft's grouping explains why early investigations mentioned both terms together; the separation after review shows that this explanation is not yet sufficient to plan subsequent changes.

## Retained Counterexamples

If catalog selection happens only when storage is created, then the claim that "batches are determined by catalog resolution" is too broad. Conversely, even if batch writes ultimately use a selected provider, that alone does not prove that catalog resolution participates in every merge. Neither direction can be inferred from the current path itself.

This record previously compressed that uncertainty into a broad judgment that the two were "in the same flow." It now explicitly leaves two questions open: where the batch boundary is formed, and when catalog resolution makes its selection. They may ultimately prove to be related, or they may have no direct relationship.

## Provisional Conclusion

Keep both items in the same historical record solely because they were raised together in the same round of requirements discussion. Defer implementation decisions: do not judge provider catalog resolution by the location of `DBStorage.h`, and do not judge the atomic scope of atomic JSON batch merge by the name provider catalog resolution.

ASR-206 are navigation entry points for the batching issue. Subsequent entries on catalog selection have not yet been added to this version, to avoid retroactively inserting objects that appeared later into this review.
