# History of Batch Processing and Provider Catalogs

This record was not removed because the early "same chain" judgment still explains why atomic JSON batch merge and provider catalog resolution were closed out in the same round. It can no longer be treated as a conclusion about their implementation relationship. The old judgment, subsequent changes, and the parts that still remain unfilled are retained below; when reading, do not focus only on the two words in the title.

## Starting point: tying the two issues together

The initial draft dealt with a very broad scope: on one side, whether JSON batch merging preserved atomic boundaries; on the other, whether provider catalog resolution could already provide a stable choice. The initial decision was to merge the records and begin the review from `packages/async-storage/windows/code/DBStorage.h`.

The thinking at the time was straightforward: batch operations ultimately have to land on some storage provider, so catalog selection should explain where the batch goes; since both concerned storage, starting from the same declaration could avoid one trip back. This idea was later shown to be unable to support the weight of meaning originally assigned to it, but it is why this page exists.

The initial draft compared only two options. One was to leave batch semantics and catalog selection separate and blank, recording them after each call site was found; the other was to write them as one bundle first and then separate them based on the object relationships near the path. The initial draft chose the latter and mistakenly wrote "close them out together first" as "they can already be explained together."

The original wording of the old decision was based not on an excerpted implementation or a complete call validation, but on the issue names, the context of closing them out in the same round, and the Windows-side path. This was a very narrow basis. When someone later continues looking for code based on this record, they should treat it as historical navigation, not as proof that batch processing and the catalog necessarily share a control point.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Merged record
  Merged record --> Batch pending investigation
  Merged record --> Catalog pending investigation
  Batch pending investigation --> Relationship judgment deferred
  Catalog pending investigation --> Relationship judgment deferred
```

The two "pending investigation" states in the diagram do not mean that the work is complete. They are the minimal correction later made to the initial draft: confirm the objects separately first, and only then discuss whether an intersection exists.

## Old position: retained, but no longer applicable

The following judgment is old and is retained here to prevent later readers from thinking it never existed.

> atomic JSON batch merge can be explained together through the path of provider catalog resolution; finding a declaration relationship near `DBStorage.h` is sufficient to determine the ownership of both requirements.

This statement is no longer applicable. It conflated "suitable as a starting point for reading" with "sufficient to determine ownership," and it also interpreted the simultaneous appearance of two names as a direct technical relationship. The path can still be used to review the local declarations and adjacent navigation from that time; it does not provide a complete account of the batch call, nor a complete account of when catalog selection occurs.

More specifically, the old position omitted two different questions. atomic JSON batch merge first requires knowing where the batch begins and when it is processed as a whole; provider catalog resolution, in contrast, first requires knowing when the catalog participates in selection and who uses the selection result. Without these two sets of material, one cannot move from "both concern storage" to "the same mechanism is responsible."

The old position also created a bad reading habit: seeing the catalog and using it to explain the batch, or seeing the batch and inferring the catalog backward. Neither inference left sufficient call records on this page to support it. This gap is not a wording issue; it is an object relationship that was not filled in at the time.

## Batch gap left by ASR-206

Later organization used ASR-206 as the investigation entry point for the current behavior of atomic JSON batch. The card description requires recovering the actual call for the most recent report of "atomic JSON batch merge" and restoring both the calling method and the result seen by the user. This requirement itself shows that the old record did not preserve those two key pieces of material.

After the release classification, one point about batch merging remains unconfirmed. This sentence about an unconfirmed point is not expanded into a specific failure, nor is it used to guess that the merge failed, the order changed, or a value was overwritten; the existing text does not provide those details. The only decision that can be retained is this: continue verifying the batch issue through the actual call and the user-facing result, and no longer substitute the catalog-selection title for this step.

This also changes how `DBStorage.h` is used. It remains the path referenced by the old investigation record and is suitable for helping readers return to the Windows-side declaration from that time; however, while the batch call has not been restored, it cannot be written as the final location of the batch semantics. Earlier versions moved too quickly through this step, and later work should not repeat the same shortcut.

One old approach was therefore discarded: write out the conclusion for the batch issue first, then treat catalog selection as supplementary context. That approach might appear to make the pre-release record more complete, but in practice it would conceal the unconfirmed calling method behind a conceptual description. The only status retained now is "the batch boundary must be confirmed by the actual call"; no merge details are to be fabricated.

## Follow-up note on catalog selection

ASR-222 were later given a security classification and moved from pending to in progress. The text left afterward still states that one point in provider catalog resolution is unconfirmed and awaits another colleague rerunning it through the same entry point. The point here is not to interpret the status transition as meaning that the cause has already been located, but to record that catalog selection did not automatically become clear merely because the batch issue was organized separately.

Therefore, this page no longer accepts either of two simplified statements.

The first is "the catalog already exists, so the selection has been determined." The existence of a catalog and how a particular selection occurs are not the same judgment. The second is "the batch has already been discussed, so the catalog must have participated in that operation." Discussing the batch and catalog participation are also not the same judgment. Both were once implicit in the merged wording of the initial draft and should now be explicitly ruled out.

The decision in this round is to defer recombining the two requirements into a single implementation decision. They remain on the same page to preserve their historical parallel relationship; they remain under separate investigation so that the historical parallel relationship is not mistaken for a call chain. This decision does not claim that they ultimately have no relationship; it only decides not to state a relationship while the respective local material is missing.

ASR-222 is the navigation entry point for the catalog-selection issue. The unconfirmed item it leaves cannot cancel out the unconfirmed item in ASR-206: the former does not answer the batch boundary, and the latter does not answer when catalog resolution occurs. After filling in either one, return to the other to confirm whether this page's old judgment needs to be updated.

## Boundaries overlooked at the time

The initial draft treated "atomic" as a sufficiently broad concept, assuming that as long as the discussion concerned a batch of JSON values, how the catalog was selected naturally belonged to the same decision. During the later review, the issue was broken down further: processing a batch of values as one boundary and selecting a provider are adjacent but distinct events. They may also leave evidence at different layers.

Likewise, the initial draft treated "catalog" as a term broad enough to encompass all backend selection details. That interpretation was too broad. The existing material only allows confirmation that it is a topic requiring further verification; it does not allow us to state the catalog's specific rules, selection order, or fallback conditions. The early wording on this page gave readers the mistaken impression that these rules had already been confirmed near the path.

There is also one adjacent question that was not separated out: if the actual call is restored, should the record first preserve the batch shape passed in by the caller, or first preserve the result seen by the user? ASR-206 require both to be restored, but this page contains no material to determine which better explains the atomic boundary. This question remains here solely because it explains why the old record cannot be considered complete after adding a few conceptual sentences.

## Decisions that can be executed now

1. Do not delete the merged judgment from the initial draft, but mark it as having been overturned by subsequent review when citing it.
2. Treat atomic JSON batch merge as an independent verification subject for ASR-206; the batch section can be updated only after the actual call and the result seen by the user have been restored.
3. Treat provider catalog resolution as an independent verification subject for ASR-222; for now, retain only its status of having one point that remains unconfirmed.
4. Until both records are complete, do not write `DBStorage.h` as the shared implementation ownership of the two requirements, and do not treat their appearance on the same page as evidence that they necessarily share a decision point.

These four items are not final rulings on implementation behavior, but rulings on how to use this old decision record. They leave the now-invalid merged position in place while preventing later readers from deriving broader conclusions from it.

## Archival notes

DOC-20 concern another set of interface review topics and are not to be merged with the batch and catalog history here. The two documents can navigate to each other, but neither page can be used to fill in the missing call material on the other.

If the calling method and user result required by ASR-206 are later restored, or the rerun result awaited by ASR-222 is obtained, directly rewrite the corresponding subsection rather than restoring "same chain" as the default explanation. The old judgment is retained to explain the path taken at the time, not to let it continue determining subsequent work.

title: Failure Context and Read-Only Removal Proposal

versions.body:
# Failure Context and Read-Only Removal Proposal

Don't combine the two issues around StorageEngine.js into one yet: backend failure context concerns what callers can see when the read path fails; read-only removal reports concern what records a removal operation leaves under read-only conditions. Treating both as "exception reports" would simplify the interface surface, but could make it easy to conflate backend read failures with removal refusals during investigation.

The tentative approach is not to add a unified report object yet. Reads would continue collecting failure context around the backend's `read`; read-only removal would retain only the operation result, pending confirmation from callers on whether they need the same display format. This keeps the change small and doesn't force existing callers to understand both types of information at once.

The risk is that the two paths may each end up growing their own fields. If we later find that callers can distinguish read failures from read-only refusals only by guessing, we'll withdraw this lightweight approach and define a shared minimum boundary first. We don't yet have enough material to decide whether reports should include raw backend information, the operation name, or key values.

# Failure Context and Read-Only Removal Proposal

The original idea was to put read failures and read-only removal in the same exception report, then have callers distinguish them by operation type. Review showed that this premise doesn't hold: the read path is concerned with backend failure context, while the removal path is concerned with read-only removal reports. Both relate to StorageEngine.js, but there's no reason to require them to share a return shape up front.

ASR-207 has been marked `failure_classified`. That mark only indicates that read failures have entered classification review; it does not mean the report fields are finalized. The check proposed in ASR-223 likewise only asks for recording what read-only removal actually returns or throws through the public entry point. Keep both cards as navigation aids, without turning their checks into interface commitments yet.

I suggest splitting the trial into two brief observation tracks:

- Preserve backend error context where reads fail, and confirm whether callers actually need the error itself, its classification, or both.
- Record the return value or exception for read-only removal, without assuming it must borrow the description used for read failures.

The earlier draft's direction of "not adding a unified report object yet" can still serve as a way to limit the change surface, but should no longer be taken to mean that the two paths are inherently independent. What we need to compare is whether callers can still distinguish them reliably if each retains local information, and whether extracting a shared structure would present a meaning absent from one path as a generic field.

I don't recommend adding an empty error context just for symmetry yet. An empty field would mislead callers into thinking the backend was involved in the failure, while a read-only refusal may not pass through the same layer. Conversely, don't require the removal path to throw the same type of object just because the read path already has failure information.

The withdrawal condition remains clear: if callers at the public entry point have to piece together two incompatible sets of information to determine whether a read failure or a read-only refusal occurred, stop the separate trials and return to discussing a shared minimum structure. What remains unconfirmed is whether that structure should cover only these two cases or would also affect other StorageEngine operations.
versions.change_summary: Split the two observation tracks based on the review

# Failure Context and Read-Only Removal Proposal

This draft originally treated "context for read failures" and "reports for read-only removal" as a single interface-convergence problem. Feedback from the field later forced us to revise that position: the two can come up in the same review without sharing an output object. The old draft is retained here because it explains why some people still look near StorageEngine.js for a unified-report proposal.

The earlier lightweight approach was to keep collecting read-failure information alongside the backend's `read`, while retaining only the action result for read-only removal. Its advantage was fewer changes for callers; its drawback was equally straightforward: the caller Fang Ke could receive two kinds of failure information with no common vocabulary. The initial diagnosis of "insufficient fields" was inaccurate. The real risk was flattening the semantics: a backend read failure and a refusal to remove something because it is read-only are not the same kind of fact.

The `failure_classified` record from ASR–207 brought read failures under closer review, but it did not decide the return shape for us. ASR–223 still only requires observing what read-only removal reports actually return or throw through the public entry point. The two cards are therefore useful starting points for checking back, not conclusions for this proposal.

There are now three candidate directions. Only the first two were fully discussed in the old material:

1. **Keep the results separate for each path.** The read path retains backend failure context; the read-only removal path separately retains the refusal or report. The advantage is that this does not pretend the two are equivalent. The cost is that callers wanting a unified display must branch themselves.
2. **Extract a minimal shared wrapper.** The wrapper expresses only "which storage operation did not complete," with each path attaching its own information. This reduces callers' first-level decision-making, but we must first establish that every field in the wrapper applies to both paths.
3. **Keep the old unified exception-report concept.** This was once considered the least troublesome approach, but it is no longer the default. It is worth revisiting for comparison only if the two public paths genuinely need the same structure for the caller Fang Ke to consume.

"Keeping them separate" does not mean allowing arbitrary divergence. If the read path retains only a formatted string, backend failure context loses its value; if the removal path disguises a read-only refusal as a backend read failure, the report will mislead investigations. During trials, inspect the raw results callers receive before deciding whether to extract a shared layer, rather than inferring the interface shape from adjacent locations in the internal implementation.

The old draft recommended "do not add a unified report object." That statement now needs correcting: we should neither commit to a unified object nor rule one out in advance. We should first limit the candidate scope of the shared portion. The only minimal information available for comparison is the path the operation belongs to and that path's own failure information; backend error context must not be applied to read-only removal merely for convenience.

One easily overlooked migration cost is the order in which existing callers make decisions. If read failures were previously treated as ordinary empty results, a new report may change their branching; if read-only removal previously checked only success or failure, an added report should not force callers to parse read-path fields either. Thus, even if a shared wrapper proves viable, it should let callers handle the operation path first and then choose whether to read the additional content.

We recommend retaining two very small trial samples rather than immediately expanding to all StorageEngine operations:

- Obtain one failure result through the public read entry point and record the backend context directly available to the caller, without inventing classification fields.
- Obtain one read-only result through the public removal entry point and record the return value or exception the caller actually receives, without rewriting it as a read failure.

If these two samples require callers to piece together incompatible information to answer "was this a read failure or a read-only refusal," the separate-results approach should be withdrawn in favor of defining a minimal shared wrapper. If the shared wrapper can only be sustained through empty fields or ambiguous error names, it should also be withdrawn, leaving the two paths to express their results independently.

Whether the report should extend beyond these two paths to cover other operations remains unresolved. The old proposal envisioned a broader scope; the recent correction shows precisely that there is no evidence to support that extrapolation. The next review only needs to answer whether a shared wrapper genuinely reduces callers' decision-making cost. Until then, StorageEngine.js remains the place to verify these two items, not proof that a unified interface has been settled.
versions.change_summary: Correct the unified-reporting assumption and preserve the withdrawal point

title: Pre-write validation and scoped-facade troubleshooting tree

versions.body:
# Pre-write Validation and Scoped-Facade Troubleshooting Tree

If invalid input has already changed stored content, or the same scoped facade behaves inconsistently because the receiver differs at call time, start by examining the write path around StorageEngine. First preserve the input for that run, what the call returned or threw, and the storage state immediately before and after the call; don't start by attributing the issue to the backend.

## Input Rejected Too Late

If the key, value, batch contents, or existing state has already changed after invalid input is reported, check whether validation occurs before anything that could trigger a write, batch processing, or backend call. The boundary to verify here is the one before the actual change, not whether the caller can restore the state later.

When the change can be reproduced reliably, record the minimal input and the object that changed, then continue checking at the write-call boundary for StorageEngine. If storage state has not changed when the report appears, don't conclude that the scope is correct based on that alone; switch to the facade branch and confirm that the invocation method has not masked the issue.

## Facade Depends on the Receiver

If a direct call through the object works, while a retained scoped facade fails or lands in a different scope after being detached from the original receiver, execute the same entry point once with the original receiver and once without it. The two inputs must be identical; compare the scope and final state, not the shape of the returned object.

When the difference appears only after the receiver changes, check whether the facade fixed the required storage scope when it was created or rereads the receiver during the actual call. The former should not switch to another scope because the invocation form changed; the latter is a boundary that needs tightening. Until the source of the scope is confirmed, don't continue tracing the cause into the backend.

## Both Phenomena Occur

First address the validation placement before the change occurs, then repeat the receiver comparison. Otherwise, the state change caused by one invalid input will make the facade comparison meaningless. The reproduction record should state whether both conditions are present at the same time; don't split one failure into two independent conclusions.

The traceback entry point is `packages/async-storage/src/runtime/StorageEngine.js`. Focus here on where the input enters the write path and when the scoped facade fixes its scope. See DOC-22 for callback or Promise compatibility differences; they do not replace the checks here for validation before the change and receiver independence.

Stop condition: handling of invalid input ends before any possible state change, and the same scoped facade retains the same scope under both receiver invocation forms. If either condition still cannot be confirmed from the recorded observations, retain the input and state differences; do not mark them as eliminated.

# Callback and Promise Compatibility Check

Start by looking at `packages/async-storage/src/createAsyncStorage.windows.ts` for the Windows compatibility entry point. Both `createAsyncStorage(_: string)` and `getLegacyStorage()` are present here; the former is the current creation entry point, while the latter retains the legacy storage view. When migrating callback callers, don't just replace the call name. Keep one record for the success path and one for the failure path, then verify them separately against the Promise callers.

`LegacyAsyncStorageImpl` immediately follows the legacy entry point in the file. It's the object to revisit when retaining the legacy view; `AsyncStorage` is imported only as a type, while the runtime binding comes from `TurboModuleRegistry`. First confirm which view the caller receives, then decide whether to change the invocation method.

Recommended order:

1. Find call sites that still pass callbacks and mark the success and failure paths separately.
2. For the same operation, retain the Promise call site and compare the value or error the caller actually receives, rather than comparing whether the two snippets look similar.
3. If they don't match, go back to the factory and legacy-view entry points first; don't add a speculative conversion at the business call site.
4. If a restoration is needed, have the caller switch back to `getLegacyStorage()` first, narrowing the review scope back to the legacy view.

`warned`, `mod`, `error` and `resultMap` all have reference points in this file. The draft treats them only as pointers for further review of binding and result handling; it does not treat them as conclusions about callback or Promise behavior itself.

# Callback and Promise Compatibility Check

This record initially only went far enough to lead the investigation to the Windows entry point: `packages/async-storage/src/createAsyncStorage.windows.ts`. Later, when reviewing the results observed by callback users, the question was not whether the two styles could fit into the same example, but what callers actually retained after successful and failed calls. ASR-209 serves only as navigation for this review; this document continues to record which objects to follow during migration and where to retain the old path.

The filename can easily make the scope seem broader than it is. The current check covers only this Windows creation module and its immediate dependencies: it imports the `AsyncStorage` type and `AsyncStorageError`, and obtains the `TurboModuleRegistry` and `TurboModule` types from `react-native`. Do not use this as a reason to include creation processes for other platforms in the same migration batch, or attribute inconsistencies seen by callers directly to the underlying module. First separate the entry point, the returned view, and the application call sites so that the subsequent comparisons do not get mixed together.

## Where the Old Calls Lead

Before migration, two types of callers can still be found: those that use a callback as a completion notification, and those that pass Promise fulfillment or rejection to their own subsequent logic. Both types of callers may access the same storage operation, but they retain results and errors differently. During the check, first record each call site's operation, its continuation after success, and its continuation after failure; do not first wrap the callback in a Promise and then treat the wrapped behavior as the original result.

The entry-point relationships in this file can initially be recorded using the diagram below. It shows the lookup order during migration, not the runtime call stack:

```text
Before migration
callback call site
    │
    ├── Caller action after success
    └── Caller action after failure

Post-migration check
Promise call site ──> createAsyncStorage(_: string) ──> Module binding
                         │
                         └── Result and error handling locations

Restore the old path
Caller ──> getLegacyStorage() ──> LegacyAsyncStorageImpl
```

The key point in the diagram is that the old path is not treated as an unrelated copy of the implementation. `getLegacyStorage()` returns the compatibility storage view that must be retained, and `LegacyAsyncStorageImpl` identifies that view's implementation. When a call site cannot yet be changed from callback to Promise, explicitly keep it on this old view; do not let it use the new entry point for half the work and rely on a caller-built adapter to fill in the rest.

## Migration Order Starting from the Callers

List the callers first, then change the entry point. A migration batch should handle only call sites whose success and failure destinations can be clearly described. Here, "success" and "failure" refer to the two branches visible to the caller Fang Ke; they do not need to have the same subsequent code, nor do all application operations need to migrate in the same batch.

**First determine where the continuations are kept.** Callback callers often put their continuations in the callback body; Promise callers attach them to fulfillment or rejection branches. The migration record must clearly state where the original continuations reside and which Promise branches handle them after the change. If the original call site handles only success and has no failure branch, do not arbitrarily mark it as "failure handled"; that call site should remain on the list awaiting confirmation.

**Then check the returned interface.** The signature of `createAsyncStorage(_: string)` itself shows that the creation entry point accepts a string argument, but migration decisions cannot stop at the argument shape. The caller receives a `AsyncStorage` view, and what really needs comparison is how it receives a successful call and a failed call. Keeping the operation name, call site, and both branches side by side in the migration record is more useful than copying over the entire block of application code.

**Review errors separately.** The module imports `AsyncStorageError`, and the file also contains a location for `error(binding)`. These indicate that error handling has its own adjacent locations, but they do not mean that all callback errors automatically appear as the same form of Promise rejection. When reviewing a failure branch, start with the object received by the caller, look back at `error(binding)`, and then inspect the binding object; do not guess error text, error codes, or recovery results from variable names.

**Remove the old callback wrapper only at the end.** The old callback wrapper can be removed only when the caller's Promise logic handles both the success and failure branches. If only the success path has been verified, record the migration status as "success checked, failure awaiting follow-up," rather than marking the call site as complete. The observations from ASR-209 are precisely what brought this distinction to the surface: a successful call and a failed call each need to leave a visible result.

This sequence is slower than "replace callbacks globally first," but it avoids mistaking a missing failure branch for compatibility. It also allows each batch to be restored independently: unconfirmed call sites remain on the old view, and confirmed call sites do not need to be rolled back along with them.

## Locations to Revisit in the File

The creation module contains several locations that should not be conflated.

- `let warned = false;` is on line 10. It identifies an internal module state variable; the migration record only needs to note that it is adjacent to the warning path. Do not treat it as evidence of a particular callback's success or failure.
- `createAsyncStorage(_: string)` is on line 16. When a caller switches to the current creation entry point, use this location to confirm the storage view it receives and the adjacent module binding.
- `getLegacyStorage()` is on line 28. During rollback, first confirm that the caller actually obtains the old view again, rather than still holding an object created earlier.
- `LegacyAsyncStorageImpl` is on line 32. When old calls still need to be retained, continue from this type to check the scope of the compatibility view.
- `mod(binding)` is on line 38, `error(binding)` is on line 52, and `resultMap(binding)` is on line 104. These are the locations for continuing the inspection of bindings, errors, and result mapping, respectively.

These locations serve different purposes. `resultMap(binding)` can help locate where results are processed, but it does not replace the record of the caller's success branch; `error(binding)` can help investigate failure handling, but it cannot prove that the caller has handled the rejection. Keeping "location in the file" and "caller branch" in separate columns in the migration table makes it less likely that code adjacency will be recorded as a behavioral conclusion during review.

## The Old Approach Retained from the Initial Draft

The initial draft described migration in four steps: find the callback, change it to a Promise, run one successful call, and return to the old entry point if necessary. This approach is not so wrong that it needs to be deleted, but it omits a separate check for failed calls and does not explain that restoring the old entry point requires the caller to obtain the view again. Continuing to follow those four steps can produce a superficially complete state: the success branch has been changed, while the failure branch still depends on the original callback location, yet the description reads as though the entire call has been migrated.

The old approach is therefore retained as a historical record, but no longer serves as the completion criterion. The current batch must at least document success and failure separately; if either one lacks a clear destination, do not remove the callback wrapper. This change does not require all callers to use uniform error handling; it prevents unchecked branches from being treated as compatible.

Another old assumption was that "the old storage view is only for temporary investigation." This also needs to be revised. `getLegacyStorage()` and `LegacyAsyncStorageImpl` are already explicit references to the recovery entry point and the implementation location. Callers Fang Ke whose Promise branches cannot be confirmed can remain on the old view for now; this restores a complete caller-level choice, rather than piling temporary conditions into application code. Once both branches for that caller are in place, migrate it separately.

## Do Only Two Things During Rollback

When an inconsistency appears, do not expand the scope of changes first. First stop removing the callback at the current call site, then switch that call site back to `getLegacyStorage()`. After switching back, check whether it obtains `AsyncStorage` from the old view again, to avoid changing only an entry-point name in the code while the object remains fixed from an earlier creation stage.

Then record the finding beside the call site: whether the success branch is missing, the failure branch is missing, or the results received on the two sides are handled differently. If the investigation only reaches `resultMap(binding)` or `error(binding)`, record "reached the module location," rather than describing it as the root cause. The binding layer still needs to be investigated further from `mod(binding)`; this page does not fill in implementation details that have not been seen.

Rollback does not invalidate the entire batch. Call sites that have clearly migrated to Promise and had both branches checked can remain as they are; only the caller that has not yet been clearly accounted for is rolled back. This allows the next review to restart from a specific gap, rather than lumping all callback calls into a single problem again.

## The Minimum Record to Leave Before Delivery

One row per migration batch is enough, but that row should contain enough information for someone later to reopen the same call site: call location, operation, success-branch destination, failure-branch destination, whether it currently uses `createAsyncStorage(_: string)` or `getLegacyStorage()`, and whether the investigation has reached `error(binding)` or `resultMap(binding)`. There is no need to paste the entire callback and Promise code into the knowledge base.

If the caller is still on the old view, state the reason as a specific gap, such as "the failure branch has no corresponding Promise handling." If the caller has already migrated, state that success and failure have both been compared item by item. A single successful call is not enough to change the retention status of the old path.

ASR-209 currently provides only an entry point for a review and adds no new conclusions about the module. The next time the same kind of inconsistency appears, still start with the caller's two branches, then return to the factory, old view, binding, error, and result-mapping locations in this file.

# Platform Selection Diagnostics Proposal

This time, diagnostics will not take the form of a human-readable log. The proposal addresses "why the storage instance ended up on this platform or provider." Callers need to assess the selection after receiving the instance; the selection process itself stays in the creation path. The early draft put "results attached to the instance" and "a separate query" side by side too quickly, without explaining what each would retain or addressing the error path separately.

Start with a smaller trial design: the creation result retains the storage instance, and the instance exposes a read-only selection description. The description answers only for this selection; it does not promise to reproduce the entire negotiation process. The recommendation is to put the target platform, actual backend, candidate providers, and selection reason in one record. If there are no candidates or the capability requirements are not met, return a creation error, with error context still handled by the existing exception path. This prevents callers from mistaking "no diagnostic record" for "the default backend was selected." The specific public fields still need an interface review; this proposal does not decide them in advance.

There are three approaches we can compare in practice.

The first is an instance-attached result. Build the diagnostic description along with the instance when selection completes; reading it later does not trigger selection again. This is best suited to reviewing "what happened at creation time" and avoids problems caused by the environment having changed by the time of a query. The cost is that every storage instance carries a public description. If existing callers treat the returned object as a narrow interface with only read and write methods, compatibility impact may need to be checked. If the final decision is to keep selection information internal, withdraw this approach rather than bypassing interface review with extra implicit properties.

The second is a separate resolver result. Have the resolver produce a selection description first, then pass it to the storage factory to create the instance. This separates selection from instance responsibilities and makes testing candidate providers more straightforward. But callers must ensure that the result passed to the factory is the one just resolved. If the resolver can run again, changes to the platform, capability set, or registry can produce two inconsistent records. This approach is worth retaining only if the existing creation flow already has a clear resolution boundary.

The third is internal logging. This is the most conservative approach for public types and can initially help maintainers identify selection branches. But callers cannot obtain a structured result, and on failure they can only rely on error text. It works as a short-term troubleshooting tool, not as the endpoint for this round of the "diagnostics" interface. The log format must not be assumed to be a stable contract either; that would merely turn a public-interface problem into a string-parsing problem.

The review entry point remains `packages/async-storage/src/web-module/IndexedDBStorage.ts`. The direct dependencies visible at the top of the file are `import { AsyncStorageError } from "../AsyncStorageError";` and `import registry from "./IndexedDBConnectionRegistry";`. The former suggests that failure context may leave through the existing exception path; the latter suggests that selection records cannot be invented independently of the registry's actual query results. What we can confirm is these two adjacent points and the file's web storage responsibility. We cannot yet infer from the filename or an old investigation path that a public interface already exists.

The trial will initially compare only three types of output from the same creation entry point: a description when the platform is explicitly specified, a failure when platform capabilities are insufficient, and a failure when the registry has no available candidates. For each type, record the runtime environment, version used, and CI job together; do not just paste result text. Success does not mean merely "fields were returned." We also need to confirm that the backend and reason in the description match the instance that was created, and preserve the context that `AsyncStorageError` can provide on failure. If obtaining the description requires querying the registry again for the same creation, the instance-attached result approach does not hold up.

Retain one earlier assessment: logging the provider name is enough for callers to identify where the issue lies. This assessment may still be useful without a structured selection description, but it does not cover selection failures or explain platform capability conditions. If the trial shows that logs meet maintainers' needs without callers needing to read the information, the public interface can be narrowed. Until then, do not treat logging as a substitute.

The verification entry points at ASR-212 require finding callers that still use "platform selection diagnostics" and checking their actual versions, entry points, and present results. The candidate designs on this page cannot replace that verification. If the results show that callers only need error context, the public description can be narrowed; if they need selection information after creation, the instance-attached result remains the preferred approach. Handle this separately from the fair queue flush history material; DOC-26 are not selection evidence for this proposal.

Make the withdrawal conditions specific: if the read-only description on the instance breaks existing compatible storage views, or if the same input under the same version and environment cannot produce a stable combination of backend, platform, and reason, withdraw the instance-attached result approach, retain internal logging temporarily, and revisit the resolution boundary. If callers need to display candidates before creation but the existing entry point can only produce a description after creation, withdraw the "read-only instance description" scope and establish a separate pre-creation negotiation proposal. Do not fill unverifiable reasons with defaults just to keep the fields.

Three issues remain open. First, whether the public description belongs in the public instance interface. Second, whether selection reasons should be a finite enumeration or extensible text, particularly whether no candidates and capability mismatches share a reason category. Third, whether failure objects need to carry information about candidates that have not yet been selected. Until these are confirmed, do not add new calling methods or describe the local adjacency of `IndexedDBStorage.ts` as the entire factory chain.

versions.body:
# Queue Flush History Troubleshooting Tree

This page is an old troubleshooting record left over from an anomaly in a fair queue's flush history. People still refer to it, but it must not be treated as a description of the queue implementation: what could be captured at the time was a situation where the post-flush state did not match the history, and this cannot establish that every kind of queue stall occurs in the same place.

The entry point remains at `packages/async-storage/src/runtime/OperationQueue.js`. Early records focused on this file not because it had been proven to be the root cause of every problem, but because the anomaly first appeared in the form of queue history. Before starting, separate the material at hand: what one flush returned, which operations in the queue had completed, and what state the caller changed to based on that result. All three can be inconsistent at the same time; do not collapse them into "the queue is broken" at the first step.

The old draft has an easily overlooked limitation: it discusses the history of the fair queue, not whether the storage backend read or write succeeded, and it does not judge the caller's batch contents. If backend errors, caller state transitions, or another batch-processing symptom also appear during troubleshooting, write them down separately first; do not use those symptoms to substitute for the gap in this history. This may look slow, but at least the next review will still be able to identify exactly which layer was missing at the time.

## Keep the situation on its original branch

```text
Abnormal state after flush
|
+-- Usable return history available
|   |
|   +-- History is continuous, but state is inconsistent
|   |   `-- Record where the history and state interpretation connect
|   |
|   `-- History has gaps, or its order cannot be explained
|       `-- Distinguish whether the gap occurred before entering the queue or after the return
|
+-- No usable history
|   |
|   +-- Can confirm that the call entered the queue
|   |   `-- Write down the last position that can be confirmed; do not fill in the intervening steps
|   |
|   `-- Cannot confirm whether it entered the queue
|       `-- Preserve the trigger conditions; do not initially attribute it to the backend or caller
|
`-- The queue no longer advances after flush
    `-- Preserve the boundary between completed and incomplete operations; do not clear the original queue
```

"Usable return history" only means that a record for comparison can still be obtained; it does not mean that the record is already correct. First check whether it covers the area around the anomaly; if it does, then check whether the caller interpreted that same history as a different state. The first question is whether the history was left behind; the second is what happened after the return was consumed. The old draft called both of these "state anomalies," which made it easy during later review to assume that the internal order of the queue had already been confirmed.

If the history is continuous but the state is wrong, record two boundaries first: the boundary of the flush return and the boundary at which the caller changed state based on the returned history. Do not write a later normal flush down as a fix just to make the situation look clean. A later return only shows that a later call obtained a segment of history; it cannot restore missing content from the previous round or prove that the previous round's state judgment was correct.

If the history itself has gaps, do not first guess which storage operation was lost. First distinguish between two narrower cases: one, the relevant call was not included in this flush before entering OperationQueue; two, the queue had already processed it, but the return side did not leave enough history. Continue along the call entry for the first case; only for the second case should you continue examining the area around the flush return. A retry will produce new history, but it will not provide the old situation needed for this distinction, so it is not the first action here.

No history does not mean that nothing executed. If you can confirm that the call entered the queue, record the last position that can be confirmed alongside whether the queue continued to advance afterward. When the available material is insufficient, do not write "no history" as "the operation did not occur"; nor should you infer directly from the blank that it was caused by a backend read. The value of this branch is simply to preserve the starting point for the next check.

If you cannot even confirm whether the call entered the queue, stop after recording the trigger conditions and call location. Sending the problem to the backend or caller for investigation at this point is too early: there may be symptoms on both sides, but without evidence that it entered the queue, they cannot be connected into a causal chain. The old version called this branch "cannot reproduce." That wording is retained now to reflect that the material was incomplete at the time, not to elevate it into an environmental problem that has already been localized.

When the queue no longer advances, first preserve the boundary between completed and incomplete operations. Clearing the entire queue to obtain new output will make the old history and the next round of history indistinguishable; restarting a batch of operations will also overwrite the original stopping point that needs to be confirmed. The stopping condition here is specific: until the boundary has been explained, do not perform recovery actions that rewrite the original queue history. This does not say that the queue can never be recovered; it only says that this record does not contain enough material to prescribe a recovery method.

## Misreadings in the old usage

Early on, some people interpreted "trace back the operation segment that initiated the flush" as requiring an outward investigation all the way through the caller. This mixes caller state, backend reads and writes, and queue records into the same round of notes, leaving only a vague "post-flush anomaly" in the end. This old reminder is still retained, but it should be used more narrowly: first confirm which segment of queue work this return belongs to, then decide whether it is necessary to leave the area adjacent to `OperationQueue.js`.

Another misreading is to treat a single successful output as a recovery signal. For a situation with gaps in the history, new output can only add a new segment of records; for a situation where the queue has stopped advancing, it may also obscure the original completion boundary. Therefore, if the current material only shows a later success without explaining the history around the earlier anomaly, the original problem remains unconfirmed.

The old draft did not provide a way to "reset and then backfill the history"; this is not an omitted operation. Manually interpreting the original history after a reset can easily mix the new and old rounds together, and the available material also does not explain what kind of backfill would preserve the original boundaries of the fair queue. When the queue needs to be recovered, preserve the situation separately first; do not write the recovery result back as if it had been true of the original record all along.

## Later on-call note

ASR-213 is described as an abnormal state after fair queue flush history processing. After work began, this card was still required to remain open because one item was still unconfirmed; only the current segment was to be continued, with the open item left open. This note did not add a new root cause, but it limits how the document should be used: reaching a branch in the troubleshooting tree does not mean the state anomaly has been explained; without closing the gap, the conclusion cannot be finalized merely because the page already contains steps.

Later, ASR-213 was blocked because the shared test environment was temporarily unavailable. Preserve the distinction made at the time: an unavailable environment only interrupts the review; it does not mean that OperationQueue has been ruled out, nor does it mean that the caller has been ruled out. In the past, "cannot reproduce" and "environment unavailable" were often written in the same box. It was later found that this caused existing return history to be mistakenly treated as unknown as well.

When a similar symptom is received, make two independent records first. The first is whether the existing return history can cover the operations around the anomaly; this can be judged solely from the current situation. The second is whether the current environment can make the same call enter the queue again; this may be blocked by the shared environment. Do not erase the first item just because the second cannot currently be performed; nor should you assume that the repeat check in the environment has been completed just because the first item left a record.

## Parts that can still be followed

When starting from `OperationQueue.js`, first confirm that the investigation concerns flush history, not queue waiting of any kind. Once history is obtained, record "continuous but state is inconsistent" and "history has gaps" separately; when history cannot be obtained, first answer whether the call has entered the queue. When the queue stops advancing, save only the completion boundary and incomplete boundary, and avoid overwriting the old situation with a new flush.

If the issue still cannot be localized, leave the symptom from this occurrence, the return boundary, and the last confirmed position. ASR-213 is the navigation entry for this record. Until the shared test environment is restored, a review that has not been performed remains a review that has not been performed. DOC-27 covers compatibility verification for immutable batch iterables; do not bring the batch-processing judgment from there over to replace the queue-history judgment here.

# Immutable Batch Iterable Compatibility Check

The original notes only said "immutable batch iterables" and did not retain the original input for that batch. Limit the migration scope to the iterable the caller passes to batch processing, rather than expanding it into a storage backend rework.

```text
Old: caller-side batch iterable → batch processing
```

# Postmortem on a Dual-State Anomaly During Caller Integration Testing

First, preserve one observation from the incident: the same object being called showed different current revision values at two points in time. In the first record, the checkpoint token already differed from the previous record, but result ordering was later able to recover. There was no evidence at the time as to whether the storage instance had changed as a result. Continuing to retry would only overwrite the original incident conditions, so the input and entry-point version were saved first.

This anomaly is part of the example and integration samples for `async storage · Client Integration`. It preserves record differences visible to the caller Fang Ke and integration feedback; runtime internals, page states from other projects, and speculation about adjacent services are not included in this incident timeline. The early records contain no start time for the anomaly, and the results after recovery cannot be used to infer when it began.

## Incident Timeline

| Time | What was observed | Action taken at the time |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | The caller sample deviated from the original state record | Saved the original input and entry-point version |
| T+07 | storage instance could still be used normally | Narrowed the scope of impact |
| T+18 | Comparison focused on the backend contract | Paused at the current interface |
| T+31 | The user path recovered | The cause remained unconfirmed |

What was saved at T+00 was the difference between two points in time, not a completed root-cause report. The checkpoint token differs from the previous record, so the two sets of results cannot simply be combined into one continuous history. The statement "could still be used normally" at T+07 does not confirm object identity either: it only indicates that this path did not exhibit the same failure again at that time.

At T+18, the comparison had focused on the backend contract. This direction was retained because it explains why repeated attempts based on the last successful result were not continued at the time; it is not a confirmed attribution. There is not enough material to show that the contract itself changed, nor any material attributing the two states to an adjacent project. The recovery at T+31 was likewise only an instance of user-path recovery, not a substitute for confirmation of the cause.

Recovery does not mean that the cause has been confirmed. The first secondhand report contained only screenshots and lacked the account, version, and run id, so it could not explain why another path worked normally. A screenshot can show that someone saw a page, but it cannot reconstruct the request context or support an item-by-item comparison with the saved entry-point version. Cleaned-up green output cannot replace the original discrepancy record.

`docs/adj-async-storage/incidents/async-storage-client-integration-same-object-two-states.md` is the recovery page actually used by this project; the related attachments are still maintained by `adj-async-storage`. The entry point is preserved here so that later readers can return to the anomaly records retained at the time, rather than treating the recovery page's latest display as the only state during the incident.

## Comparison for Month 12

In the comparison for month 12, ASRA-012 recorded a specific difference: the internal results included "current result," while the regular entry point corresponding to the exit entry point did not. Here, "did not" describes only the difference in what the two entry points displayed at the time, and does not mean that the internal results can represent the regular entry point or that the reason the regular entry point was empty has been determined.

This difference changed how the recovery assessment was written. Previously, seeing only the internal results recover could easily lead to a record saying "the two states are now unified"; but when the regular entry point has no corresponding content, the most that can be written is that the internal results have appeared. Checking whether the displays at the two entry points are consistent requires separately preserving each entry point, its displayed content, and the time it was observed.

ASRA-012 also called for marking when the current entry point changed. Statistics from before and after the change cannot be directly subtracted from each other, because they may come from different entry points, and the values being compared may not belong to the same series. This limitation does not change the original anomaly, only how the impact window can be described: a stretch of green results from a later entry point cannot overwrite an earlier discrepancy record.

ASRA-009 recorded another inconsistency: the expiration action had already become invalid, but the entry-point prompt on the page had not yet been updated. This resembles "the internal results had content, but the regular entry point did not," in that both show that entry-point presentation and actual actions must not be treated as the same signal; the two are still not the same issue. An outdated page prompt does not establish the current revision received by the caller, nor does it by itself explain changes to the storage instance.

Therefore, this postmortem did not treat the page prompt from ASRA-009 as the cause of the failure. It is retained only as a counterexample when cross-checking entry points: a prompt that is still visible may no longer correspond to a valid action. For caller samples, the original input, entry-point version, and request context more closely reflect the incident conditions than the last prompt line on the page.

ASRA-010 confirmed this project's scope and supplied the handover, takeover, and confirmation times as supplementary information. The handoff adds recordkeeping context, not a new technical conclusion. Before writing "recovered," it must first be possible each time to answer: which entry point was viewed, which version of the input was used, and under what conditions further attempts were stopped. Without these materials, the recovery record can only be retained as a partial observation.

## How the Approach Was Narrowed at the Time

The first step was to stop retrying. Continuing to run until the results matched again might have produced a neater page, but would have lost the input and timing relationships from the first discrepancy. The order retained afterward was: first save the original record and entry-point version, then record the current revision and checkpoint token, and only then record result ordering after recovery.

The interpretation of "user-path recovery" as the end of the incident was also narrowed. It now means only that the caller was once again able to obtain usable results at some stage. It does not mean that the regular entry point has been updated, that the internal results and the regular entry point are aligned, or that the storage instance has been explained. Recovery, entry-point consistency, and object changes are three separate issues.

If the current revision does not match the saved record, or only screenshots remain without the original input, do not stitch the old and new states together into a single trend. If the entry point itself is found to have changed, save the before-and-after data separately; if the regular entry point and the internal results differ, retain them separately as well, without replacing either with the other. The records preserved this way will be less complete than "everything has recovered," but will not erase the differences observed at the time.

## What Remains Open

The recovery assessment that can currently be recorded is: result ordering has recovered, and the two states during the anomaly did actually appear at entry points visible to the caller Fang Ke. This cannot establish which layer the change in the storage instance originated from, nor can the old prompt at the regular entry point be treated as the current revision.

There are insufficient records of the cause, when the impact began, or when the two entry points became consistent again. Follow-up records need to check the same input through the original entry point and retain the current revision and request context; if the environment cannot access the entry point, record that the state cannot be verified rather than substituting another green output. Permission issues that arose after ASRA-011 are outside the scope of this version of the materials and must not be retroactively incorporated here.
