# Postmortem on the Dual-State Anomaly in Caller Integration Testing

The earliest record was not a complete conclusion about the incident, but a narrowly scoped field note: real call samples built around example and integration showed different current revisions at two points in time. The adaptation boundary, integration feedback, maintainers, and exit criteria all fall within `async storage · Client Integration`'s own scope of work. The status of adjacent projects cannot be used to fill the gaps in this record.

At the first save, the checkpoint token already differed from the one in the old record. The original entry point was not overwritten, and further retries were stopped. At that moment, all that was known was that the displayed state had changed, not whether the change had occurred in the caller sample, the entry-point record, or the storage instance further downstream. The missing timestamp was left as: ____. This was not a field that could be filled in from memory.

result ordering was later restored, but no evidence was found to explain why the storage instance changed. The early record placed these two points in the same paragraph, which could make "the path recovered" look like "the object had returned to its original state". The later addendum retained the original field assessment and only separated the two: recovery is a caller-side outcome, while the cause and object identity remain open questions.

## The Initially Observed States

At the time, both the entry point and the record page pointed to the same caller integration test sample, but they showed different current revisions at two points in time. To avoid treating the last line of results on the page as the full incident context, the original input, entry-point version, and recovery page were retained together in the project's own incident-export. The path for the long-term documentation is `docs/adj-async-storage/incidents/async-storage-client-integration-same-object-two-states.md`; this path documents this project's anomaly, not an overview of the main runtime project.

The early assessment was cautious: the different checkpoint tokens meant that the records seen on the two occasions could not be directly stitched together; the fact that result ordering could be restored meant that at least part of the caller path later became available again; whether the storage instance had been replaced still could not be determined from those few lines. At that time, the backend contract was not cited as the cause, nor were the messages on the regular entry point treated as confirmation.

The original screenshot-based account later proved insufficient. It contained only the image, with no account, version, or run id, so it could not explain why another path was still working normally. The screenshot could be retained as an incident attachment, but could not replace the input and entry-point version. This distinction only became important after recovery: looking only at the green result would hide the fact that two states had once coexisted in the surrounding context of this record.

The first record also mixed terminology from three levels: the results seen by the caller, the records shown by the entry page, and the storage instance. On later review, this mixing could make a visible difference read as an object change. The current version does not delete the terms from the old record, but places them back at the appropriate observational level before each assessment: a difference at the entry point is a saved observation; recovery of the user path is the result of subsequent actions; whether the object changed remains an unanswered question.

## What Preserving the Timeline Means

| Time point | What was observed at the time | Subsequent action |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | The caller sample differed from the original state record | Save the original input and entry point version |
| T+07 | The storage instance was still usable as normal | Narrow the scope of impact |
| T+18 | Comparison pointed to backend contract | Stop at the current interface without attributing a cause |
| T+31 | The user path was restored | Separate restoration from confirmation of the cause |

T+00 does not mean that the anomaly's start time was already known, only that this was when the difference was first recorded. There is no complete timeline leading up to it, so T+00 cannot be treated as the start of the impact. No earlier time point was fabricated later, nor were update times from other pages used to fill this gap.

The observation at T+07 also needs to be preserved with its original meaning. The storage instance was still usable at the time, which does not mean it was necessarily the same as the object in the old record; it only narrowed the scope of impact from the conjecture that "the object is already unavailable" to "the states visible to caller Fang Ke differ". This step prevented a record issue from being inflated into a total storage outage.

At T+18, backend contract was the focus of the comparison. This focus shows that the investigators tried to examine the caller's records alongside the interface contract, and does not mean that the contract had been proven to have changed. There was not enough input to attribute the two states to the contract, the entry point, instance replacement, or adjacent services. The old version made it sound like a conclusion, while the current version explicitly retains it as the focus of comparison at the time.

The restoration of the user path at T+31 likewise cannot replace the preceding three items. The result ordering after restoration can be added to the timeline as an interim outcome; but the recovery page having results, the standard entry point showing a prompt, the two entry points using the same record, and the storage instance having been explained are all separate propositions. They cannot be merged into "the incident is over" simply because they all occur after restoration.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Observed: Records at the two points in time differ
    Observed --> Preserved: Preserve the original input and entry version
    Preserved --> Compared: Compare against the current entry
    Compared --> Restored: result ordering restored
    Compared --> Unconfirmed: Cause or object change unconfirmed
    Restored --> Unconfirmed: Restoration does not equal attribution
    Unconfirmed --> Compared: New on-site evidence
```

This state diagram only describes how this record remains "unconfirmed"; it does not represent a new execution flow. In particular, the line from Restored to Unconfirmed preserves the distinction most easily lost in this review: the caller can obtain the result again, but that does not answer why the current revisions at the two points in time differ.

## Entry and record are not the same signal

In the comparison from 2025 year 12 month, ASRA-012 left a concrete difference: the internal result contained "current result", while the ordinary entry corresponding to the exit entry did not. Here, "did not" describes only what was visible on the page at that time. It does not mean that the internal result can represent the ordinary entry, nor does it mean that the reason the ordinary entry lacked content has been found.

This difference overturns an overly convenient formulation: writing "the recovery page has a result" as "the two entries are already consistent". If the internal result can be displayed while the ordinary entry has no corresponding display, at most we can say that one entry has a result. Entry consistency must be recorded separately for each entry; the green status on one page cannot replace it.

ASRA-012 also requires marking the change time of the current entry. After the entry changes, the before-and-after metrics cannot be directly subtracted, because the two sets of numbers may come from different entries. This limitation does not change the anomaly itself, but it changes how the impact window is expressed: a later green record cannot cover an earlier deviation, and the two revisions cannot automatically be treated as the same continuous sequence.

There was initially an impulse that was not retained: to infer the earlier record from the last current revision that appeared on the page. This approach was not adopted. What the current entry displayed later cannot prove what the earlier entry displayed; even less can it prove that the checkpoint token difference was caused merely by a page refresh. The reason for saving the entry version is precisely to avoid backfilling a later display into the earlier state.

The subsequent records for ASRA-009 showed another similar but not identical mismatch: the action had already expired and was no longer valid, but the entry-point message on the page had not yet been updated. This shows that page messages and valid actions do not always convey the same signal. This observation can help readers understand why the message text is not being used to confirm the current state in this incident, but it is not a cause of the storage instance change.

The two entry-point discrepancies cannot be conflated. The difference between the internal result and the display at the standard entry point is a difference in page content observed in the comparison; the action being invalid after expiry while the message remains unchanged is a mismatch between action and message. Together, they limit what the page can prove, but they do not jointly establish the same type of failure. Presenting them as a single root cause would take this project's localized anomaly beyond what the available material supports.

## Why the initial recovery assessment was insufficient

Initially, the easiest approach to adopt was to keep retrying based on the last successful result until the two states aligned again. It seemed capable of quickly making the page consistent again, but it would overwrite the inputs and timing relationships from the first deviation. Continued retries were no longer treated as the preferred action; preserving the original records first became the handling approach actually retained for this incident.

The records were not preserved to make the material appear complete, but because the initial secondhand report contained only screenshots. The screenshots lacked the account, version, and run id, so they could not reconstruct the request context or explain why another path was still working normally. With only a screenshot, all that can be confirmed is that someone saw a particular display at a particular time; one cannot confirm whether it shares a source with the earlier records, let alone use it to replace the original input.

The green result after recovery poses another problem: it makes "the user path is usable again" and "the anomaly has been explained" look like the same statement. The assessment actually retained is narrower. The fact that result ordering can be restored means that at least part of the caller path can once again produce the expected order; there is still no evidence as to why the storage instance appears different.

Therefore, the recovery page does not establish a root-cause conclusion. It preserves the original entry point, input, record version, and subsequent recovery context. Each time this page is revisited, the first distinction to make is whether the material being viewed was retained during the incident or is the current display provided by the entry point after recovery. Both may be useful, but neither can substitute for the other.

The statement in the old records that "the comparison points to the backend contract" was also narrowed in this round. It remains on the timeline to explain why the investigation stopped at the current interface at the time; it has not been elevated to a causal attribution. The available material does not establish that the contract itself changed, nor does it establish that this line of inquiry explains the two revisions. Rewriting this statement directly as a root cause would overwrite what was actually unknown at the time with a later reconstruction.

## The handoff supplied conditions, not answers

ASRA-010 confirmed the scope of `async storage · Client Integration` and provided the handover, takeover, and confirmation times as supplementary information. What was added here was not another technical assessment, but a set of conditions that allowed the incident context to continue to be checked: which entry point to use, which version of the input to preserve, and at what point to stop further attempts.

These conditions mean that "recovery" is no longer just a final screenshot. The person taking over needs to be able to distinguish: whether what is currently visible is the normal entry point or an internal result; which entry point the current revision was read from; and which prior record the checkpoint token differs from. Omitting any one of these could combine page content from two unrelated points in time into a single change.

Leaving stop conditions in the on-call handoff also prevents the scope from continuing to expand when the evidence is insufficient. If all that remains are screenshots, or if the current revision does not match the saved version, stop the record at the point where the observed state is saved; do not treat the latest page as a successful reproduction. If the normal entry point and the internal result differ, save both separately; do not select the one that looks more normal as the sole source of truth.

This restriction applies only to this project's caller integration-testing samples. It does not require other storage integrations to use the same recording method, nor does it interpret lag at this project's entry point as a general runtime problem. example, integration, and integration feedback remain the boundary here; beyond these objects, this document does not continue to draw inferences.

## Process of narrowing the impact scope

The impact that can be confirmed is very limited: in this project's caller integration-testing samples, the same object showed different current revision values at two points in time, and at least one entry-point result later recovered. Here, "same object" comes from the association between the entry point at the time and the record page; it does not mean that the identity of the underlying instance has been confirmed.

The parts that cannot be confirmed must also be stated clearly. No evidence establishes when the anomaly began; no evidence shows whether the missing display at the normal entry point is related to the storage instance; and no evidence shows that all callers encountered the same state. Describing the impact as "all callers are affected" goes beyond the sample, while describing it as "just a page prompt" would erase the difference between the checkpoint token and the current revision.

The failed expiration action and the not-updated prompt in ASRA-009, and the difference between the internal result and the normal entry point in ASRA-012, all belong to the layer where entry-point behavior requires separate verification. They help constrain the conclusion; they cannot be combined into a single cross-project failure thread. The status of adjacent projects, results from other user paths, and internal runtime explanations are all outside this impact scope.

DOC-32 is the checklist for adjacent exit windows. When an exit action needs to be checked, you can navigate there from here, but it does not replace this anomaly's timeline or the original records of the two states. An exit-action failure and the caller sample's observation of different revision values may appear together in adjacent materials, but they cannot therefore be written up as having the same cause.

There is still a gap in the impact window: the start time preceding the initial discrepancy was not retained. The current version has not used the entry-point comparison time, the page-prompt failure time, or the later recovery time associated with ASRA-012 to fill that gap. Those times each describe a different action; combining them would create an incident start that looks precise but is actually unsupported.

## Changes captured in subsequent reviews

Before the third version was finalized, another timing relationship appeared in the separate event timeline for ASRA-011: the recorded expiration action occurred before the original input. This record does not revise the account of this anomaly, but it reminds us that the order of the cards may not match the order of the original inputs. If a summary written later conflicts with the saved input, it must not override the earlier evidence simply because it was updated more recently.

This also explains why this page continues to retain the original inputs and entry point versions, rather than only the card summaries. Cards can point to areas requiring review, such as the separate event timeline, expiration actions, or entry point changes; the original inputs remain the evidence for determining the context in which the two states appeared. When the two conflict, recording the conflict itself is closer to reality than forcing them into a single timeline.

ASRA-011 later moved to blocked, with the recorded reason that the account provided by the caller did not have permissions in this environment. This result explains why some branches could not be reviewed further, but it does not explain the initial two states. The permissions blocker should be classified as "unable to review", not retroactively recorded as "the original anomaly was caused by permissions".

The permissions issue also changed the boundaries of subsequent actions. When the environment lacks permissions, another green output cannot replace the check at the original entry point, nor can success with another account justify declaring that the same object has been verified. We should retain the blocking fact, preserve the existing inputs, and acknowledge that this branch was not reproduced. This is more accurate than misreporting differences in permissions as differences in state.

# Alternative Approach for Caller Integration Testing

This draft was not adopted as the integration approach. It preserves a disagreement at the time over async-storage-client-integration: whether the results seen by integrators should remain tied to `validation report`, or be split out of the validation report and handled separately.

I initially favored the former. The existing entry point already provided validation information, so callers would not have to interpret two sets of results. If the only difference was in the input-check messages, that choice seemed sufficient. But on reviewing the working draft, the two processing paths had different failure exits. Calling both of them validation reports would lead integrators to conflate "receiving a report" with "how this call ends."

## Approaches proposed at the time

**Keep the existing route.** Callers would continue to receive only `validation report`, with no change to the existing entry point. The benefit was a small change footprint, with no need to agree on another caller-facing description. The problem was that once the failure exits differed, callers could only infer subsequent behavior from the report contents; the draft did not make clear whether that inference was reliable.

**Split out caller-visible behavior.** The validation report would still describe input checks, while the results callers actually needed to assess would be listed separately. This was not a proposal to rework validation, but to avoid collapsing two exits into a single concept. I leaned toward this route at the time, based only on the differences already present in the draft; it had not been confirmed that all callers needed it.

This was also why it was not adopted: the existing callers of `provider catalog` had not yet been identified. Without knowing who only read the validation report and who already depended on the old entry point, the split would turn a local cleanup into an integration risk. The original input should still be retained; a similar sample must not be created just for the experiment.

## Withdrawal conditions

Work would not proceed if the existing callers of `provider catalog` could not be found, or if the separated behavior merely duplicated `validation report` without giving callers a new basis for a decision. Whether withdrawal would mean only restoring the old entry point had not been decided at the time; the attachments also did not contain enough information to say whether the integration agreements built around the old entry point would need to be addressed.

## Still undecided

- Whether `provider catalog` is actually read by current callers;
- Whether any adapters outside the old entry point already depend on the same failure exit;
- Which description to retain after withdrawal so callers do not think the route has already taken effect.

The draft is still at `docs/adj-async-storage/proposals/unadopted-async-storage-client-integration-route.md`. The "preference for splitting" here was the judgment at the time, and should not be treated as an interface definition that was subsequently implemented.

# Release Automation Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

The anomaly occurred in the build queue formed around `.github/workflows` and `release`. The same release automation object appeared in two states at the current entry point: the first check returned one current revision; after the recovery action, reopening the entry point returned another current revision. The original record, recovery page, and artifact version were not merged into a single new record during the incident.

The main impact was on determining the withdrawal window. As the queue continued to advance, the revision displayed on the second visit alone could not establish which artifact version was still eligible for withdrawal; the two states were also not enough to show that the release had recovered. Further retries were therefore stopped at that point, preserving the existing state to prevent new build results from overwriting the first observed object state.

## Sequence of Events

- On the first comparison, the operation queue did not match the old record. The discrepancy first showed up as a change in the current revision displayed at the entry point, not as a single workflow file disappearing.
- The original record was kept at `docs/adj-expo-with-async-storage/incidents/expo-with-async-storage-release-automation-same-object-two-states.md`. The views of the build queue, artifact version, and withdrawal window from that time were all saved there.
- Afterward, the checkpoint token could still be used on the recovery page. This result only showed that the recovery entry point could still return a response; it was not enough to treat the two states as consecutive results from the same release run.
- After the second read, the result ordering differed from the earlier record. It was not confirmed during the incident whether this was due to a sampling change, the queue recovery order, or a change in the entry point's display.

The provisional assessment at the time was to treat the discrepancy as a post-recovery change in queue ordering. That assessment is retained here because no record was obtained that could link both current revisions to the same artifact version; it should not be treated as a fixed explanation for later releases.

## Records After Stopping

The handoff was updated with the version, request context, and stop conditions to avoid relying only on the last line of green output. The successful recovery result was saved alongside the original failure window, without writing back to the original object's state. It remained unconfirmed what the artifact version actually belonged to, what caused the ordering change, and whether the withdrawal window also changed with the second state.

If the same entry-point discrepancy appears again, you should first save the first current revision shown on each side of the change, then check the original record and recovery page separately; do not interpret a difference in counts directly as recovery.

If an exit action has already changed the queue or artifact state, but there are not enough records to establish the next step, stop taking further actions. Preserve the state and refer the gap in execution records to the relevant owner for assessment. Without records that can be checked, do not rerun anything to manufacture an apparently complete final state.

5. **Keep a minimal record after closing the window.** Record the `batch boundary` found this time, the last visible result, whether an execution record was found, and one of "Exited," "Withdrawn," or "Undetermined." Neither of the first two is equivalent to a successful release. For a window with no records, state only that its status cannot be determined; do not fill the gap with explanatory text.

The follow-up checks in ASRC-003 are for investigating gaps in the current revision; if an execution record still cannot be found, keep the status as "Undetermined." For ASRC-006, retain only this page's timeline. Put only a link in the daily report, and do not merge results from adjacent entries into this entry.

# Alternative Approaches for Release Automation

The release queue originally tracked the trigger entry point, artifact version, and rollback decision together in a single record flow. One proposed approach is to split out the rollback decision and save it as a separate record alongside the artifact version; the other is to leave them together, with the workflow entry point continuing to hold all three types of information.

Splitting them means that looking up an artifact version no longer requires searching backward from the end of the queue, and the rollback window has its own place. The trade-off is that the entry-point record and the new record may change independently. Whether the two will still line up after the entry point changes remains unanswered; if only the final state is copied, the decision from the old entry point will also be lost.

We can't say yet which approach is better. We first need to retain the original input, the artifact version, and the rollback decision as first observed, then check whether the records in the two locations still match. One successful release does not show that the split is effective, because it only proves that the queue can run to completion.

Two questions remain unresolved: whether a rollback should restore the workflow entry point or the independent record; and whether intervening windows with no records should be left as missing or may be backfilled from the release queue. Until the backfill rules are settled, do not describe the proposed approach as an active release method. The reference material is at `docs/adj-expo-with-async-storage/proposals/unadopted-expo-with-async-storage-release-automation-route.md`.

# Candidate Approaches for Release Automation

The earlier split proposal was: the release entry would continue to trigger the workflow, while another record would store the artifact version and rollback window. It remains only a trial candidate, not an entry that has already been switched over. The new check is not whether the records look tidy, but whether the two segments can still be compared correctly after the entry changes.

The historical actions of ASRC-007 make this concrete: when starting to compare trends before and after the unadopted approach, the change point for the current entry must be marked separately. The statistics before and after the change cannot be subtracted directly. If the new record starts being written only after the switch, the trend chart will connect results produced by two different entries into a single line; if both sides are written, it will also be necessary to state which segment belongs to the old entry. The candidate approach does not yet resolve this boundary.

After ASRC-001 was classified as a release issue, the routing of the old exit action still needs to be reviewed against the pre-change snapshot. A split record can store the artifact version, but it cannot replace this snapshot. Copying the snapshot into an independent record also cannot guarantee that the old route's decision retains its original context, so the rollback location cannot be selected solely by the "latest record."

The recovery scenario rules out another seemingly convenient workaround. The records for ASRC-004 require taking only the first current revision from the recovery point onward and ignoring subsequent aggregation initially. If the candidate approach waits until aggregation at the end of the queue before adding the rollback record, it will mix the first record after recovery with the results aggregated later. Even with complete aggregation, it would then be impossible to say which record was the decision actually visible at the time of recovery.

The trial therefore keeps only a small window: for the same release input, the existing entry continues to leave a queue segment, while the candidate record separately stores the artifact version and rollback window. The comparison checks whether the entry switch point is marked, whether the first current revision after recovery can be located, and whether rollback can still return to the original entry. Neither side changes the user, input, or observation window; the first visible result is saved first.

A single green run, changing only the display label, or being unable to restore the original entry during rollback does not count as success. If lookup speed does not improve, or if the records lack the intermediate window and can only be completed through later aggregation, end the trial and restore the original entry. It remains undecided whether the rollback window should become an independent field and whether a period with no record should remain empty permanently.

# Proposal for an Alternative Release Automation Approach

This record began with a lookup problem: as the release queue grew, artifact versions, rollback windows, and the rollback decisions made at the time were crowded around the workflow entry point. Reviewing a batch of releases meant searching backward through the queue. The candidate approach moved rollback decisions into a separate record, leaving the entry point responsible only for triggering releases; the separate record kept versions and windows together. The other approach retained the existing entry point without adding a parallel record.

The split initially seemed clearer, but it depended on a mapping that had not been established at the time: a version in the separate record had to be traceable to the entry point that produced it, the boundary between before and after entry point changes, and the routes available to the rollback action at the time. Without that mapping, the new page would just be another place to look, not an additional source of reliable history.

The first issue raised in review was the entry point switch. The action in ASRC-007 was to compare trends before and after the approach that was not adopted, with a requirement to mark when the current entry point changed. The before-and-after statistics cannot simply be subtracted from each other. Queue segments written by the old entry point and version records written by the new record cannot automatically form a continuous trend, even if their fields look similar. The candidate approach had treated "saving a separate copy" as an improvement; after this counterexample, saving a separate copy was no longer a success criterion in itself.

Another counterexample came from the exit action. ASRC-001 recorded residual routing to the old exit action. The approach was to remove actions pointing to the old action while retaining a pre-change routing snapshot. If the separate record became the only lookup point during a rollback, it could tell people the artifact version but could not replace the old entry point snapshot. Copying the snapshot to both places would create two sets of material whose order would need to be determined. The rollback window therefore could not be reconstructed solely from the last line of the separate record.

The read order during recovery could not be resolved through later summaries either. The historical action in ASRC-004 corresponds to "the first record for the current revision after recovery" and requires taking only the first record for the current revision from the recovery time onward, leaving later summaries aside initially. The candidate approach had considered waiting for summaries from later in the queue to backfill the separate record. That backfill plan was dropped because it would combine the first record visible at recovery with conclusions from later summaries in a single assessment, making it impossible to reconstruct the entry point's state at the time.

| Option | Local capabilities retained | Main cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Continue using the release entry point | The queue, artifact versions, and rollback decisions remain in one place | Slower lookups as the queue grows |
| Split out a separate rollback record | Versions and rollback windows can be viewed side by side | Entry point switches, old routes, and recovery order must be aligned across records |

The second option in the table was not adopted. Dropping it did not mean the entry point would never need reorganizing; there simply were not sufficiently stable mapping rules at the time. Once the separate record was treated as the sole source, entry point change times would be hidden, the old exit action would become detached from its snapshot, and the first record after recovery could also be overwritten by later summaries. Keeping the entry point made lookups cumbersome, but it was easier at the time to preserve the relationships as they stood.

The trial discussion later narrowed to a small window. With the same release inputs, the existing entry point would retain queue segments, while the candidate record would append only the artifact version, rollback window, and first visible decision. One passing release would not establish that the approach worked; a single green result, no real users, changes limited to display labels, or an inability to return to the original entry point on exit would not count as success. The comparison had to answer three questions: whether the periods before and after an entry point change were mistakenly treated as one trend, whether the first record for the current revision after recovery could still be located, and whether the original entry point could still be found during rollback.

ASRC-013 limited what "backfilling intermediate records" could mean. It left this task open: `- [ ] Align expo-with-async-storage-release-automation with the current entry point, leaving windows with no records empty`. Missing windows therefore cannot be inferred from adjacent versions or filled in with results from later summaries. An empty record is itself retained as the observed state until new entry point material can explain what happened during that period.

There was also a separate stop point near the rollback deadline. ASRC-010 required contacting the original owner before the exit action expired; if there was no reply, close out using the existing exit action. The candidate approach could not use expiration as an opportunity to switch to the new record, nor could it interpret no reply as consent to migrate. This stop point kept rollback handling at the original entry point, avoiding a change in record location precisely when preserving the old context mattered most.

The decision in this record is therefore to retain the existing release entry point, not create a separate rollback record, and not treat this abandoned proposal as a plan for automatic resubmission. If the approaches are compared again later, the material must include, together, at least the entry point change time, the corresponding artifact version, the first record for the current revision after recovery, the pre-change snapshot of the old exit action, and the missing windows. If these objects cannot be linked in a single relationship that can be reviewed later, the approach should remain a candidate rather than switching first and backfilling records afterward.

The related entry point is `docs/adj-expo-with-async-storage/proposals/unadopted-expo-with-async-storage-release-automation-route.md`. ASRC-001, ASRC-004, ASRC-007, ASRC-010, and ASRC-013 serve only as entry points for revisiting their respective local contexts; they do not recast the unadopted approach as the current release rules.

# On-Call Procedure for a Failed Compatibility Catalog Run

This page records the on-call actions for a single `gradle-compatibility-catalog` run. The entry point is still `docs/adj-gradle/runbooks/gradle-compatibility-directory-failed-run-on-call-page.md`; if the message does not provide this entry point, the original input, or an identifiable version, stop first. Do not reconstruct the incident using similar input.

## Preserve the Incident State

After receiving a report of an abnormal run, first collect the current state of `gradle-compatibility catalog-on-call page for a failed run`, the original input, and the `storage instance` version in one place. Preserve the result you saw initially as well. The normal results compiled on the page later may only be used for comparison; they must not overwrite the original record of the failed run.

Locate `checkpoint token` through the entry point, then inspect what follows the location where it appears. If `checkpoint token` is not in the entry point, stop and record "token not found at entry point"; do not continue guessing `result ordering`. If the token appears but `result ordering` differs from the most recent known-good sample, stop at the first difference; save the raw excerpts from both sides before deciding whether any other checks are needed. A difference in sort order alone does not mean the stored content is corrupted.

Do not handle the following three situations as a single case:

- `storage instance` never appeared. Record the input, version, and entry point state, then stop. This means "this stage was not reached," not that subsequent records were lost.
- `storage instance` appeared, but the intermediate records were not retained continuously. Preserve the last visible record and the location of the gap; do not clean up or backfill a history that looks complete.
- `validation report` appeared, but there is no evidence of its relationship to the first difference. Save the report as is, and continue to use the first difference as the stopping point.

Early on-call records placed the absence of `storage instance` and the `result ordering` anomaly in the same paragraph; later replay showed that these two observations may have occurred at different stages, so they have separate stopping points here. Keep the old `journal recovery` wording, but it only indicates a recovery approach considered at the time, not that recovery has run successfully in the shared environment.

## Change Only One Condition

When verification is needed, first choose one condition: input, permissions, or version. Keep the other conditions unchanged from the most recent known-good sample. Do not refresh permissions, restart the run, and regenerate the input at the same time; even if the result is green afterward, you will not know which action changed the first difference.

If you need to reexamine the input, replay the original input associated with ASRD-011; do not create a separate, similar input. Record the replay result at the original stopping point: whether it stopped again at `checkpoint token`, `storage instance` appeared, or only `validation report` appeared. Do not write "run recovered" when you mean "replay completed."

If `storage instance` appears after changing only one condition, check whether subsequent records are still missing. A record appearing does not mean `result ordering` has recovered; record the two separately. If the sort order still differs, preserve the first sort-order difference and the new condition, and stop there. Without enough excerpts, do not proceed along the old `journal recovery`.

Change permissions only when permissions themselves are the condition being verified. Preserve the original state before changing permissions; if the entry point changes from visible to invisible afterward, record "entry point state changed." Do not treat a restricted entry point as a run failure. When rolling back, restore the original permissions; do not clean up the original input or delete the failure records.

## Scope Boundaries

This page only covers the entry conditions, first failure, stopping point, and handoff entry point for this `gradle-compatibility-catalog` run. It does not identify callers on behalf of other projects in the workspace, nor does it decide `backend contract` on behalf of the shared interface. If a difference goes beyond the scope of "cross-package dependencies, version combinations, and consumer integration formed around the workspace; with independent schedules, maintainers, and exit criteria," preserve adj-gradle's own users, incident state, and exit criteria, then hand the entry point and observed behavior to the shared interface owner.

Do not conclude that the entire adaptation chain has succeeded just because you saw `compatibility adapter`. In the old incident state, this term only marked the object that was observed. Only specific excerpts can establish whether it was before or after the first difference; without excerpts, leave this unknown.

## Handoff and Rollback

For handoff, leave only what will allow the next check to pick up where you left off:

- The file path actually accessed, and whether `checkpoint token` was found;
- Whether `storage instance` appeared, and what the last visible object was;
- The first difference in `result ordering` and the comparison sample;
- The single change made, the hypotheses ruled out, and whether the original input was retained;
- Recovery actions that remain unconfirmed and the entry point for the next check.

For the owner of `backend contract`, write only the entry point indicated by the existing material; do not fill in a name for an unknown person in charge. Preserve the original incident state even after restoring service; "green" can only be a new observation and must not overwrite the stopping point at the time of failure. If there are no new excerpts, keep statements from the context of earlier dates on file; do not rewrite them as current conclusions.

ASRD-006 can be used to review "missing intermediate records in the on-call run," and ASRD-011 can be used to review the original-input replay. DOC-44 is the adjacent comparison record for the current revision; it can help confirm the comparison target, but it cannot fill in intermediate records that were not retained during the run for this page. These entry points are for navigation only; assessments of the run must still be written beside the actual stopping point on this page.

The old page retained two unresolved terms, `release evidence` and `caller-visible behavior`. Neither led to an independent conclusion in this run: the former cannot replace the failure excerpt, and the latter cannot replace the caller's results. If there is a new replay or a new entry point later, leave new observations at the corresponding step; do not rewrite the old incident state on this page into a complete description of the compatibility catalog.

This checklist covers only the handoff at the end of the window: borrowing the current entry, the final output, the return time, and the rollback entry for adj-gradle. First open `docs/adj-gradle/release/gradle-compatibility-directory-short-checklist-before-window-end.md` and confirm that the page you have is still the current entry. Leave similarly named catalogs, outputs left over from earlier windows, and release decisions outside the scope of this borrowing out of this record.

The end of the window does not mean the release decision has been confirmed. The details kept here let the next person identify the state at handoff; any decisions not listed remain for the original owner to confirm. Record the borrowed item, final output, return time, and pre-rollback state in the order they actually occurred. There is no need to add background from earlier pages, and do not record zero results as normal results.

1. [ ] At the start of the borrowing period, record the item shown at the current entry and note the final output you plan to hand over. This borrowing record applies only to this window. If the entry won't open, or you cannot confirm that the page is still the current entry, stop the closeout. Do not substitute an alternate page or use old output to fill in this item.

2. [ ] Find `validation report` through the current entry and retain its last output. If the output already contains `caller-visible behavior`, do not delete it just to clean up after the window. Keep this result with the borrowed item so that, after it is returned, you can see what was handed over, not just the catalog.

3. [ ] Record the actual return time and confirm that the original path can still be viewed after the borrowing ends. The return record describes only what was actually borrowed this time and the return action; it does not replace release confirmation outside the window. If only a new page is visible at return time and you cannot determine whether the original path is usable, preserve the state as it is and do not mark the handoff complete.

4. [ ] Check whether `provider catalog` appears in the results associated with the current entry. If it does not, stop the release closeout. It does not establish that the catalog has recovered, and similarly named pages cannot be used as a substitute for this check.

5. [ ] If rollback is needed, start at the rollback entry for adj-gradle. First undo the temporary handoff caused by this round of borrowing, then retain the last output before rollback and the recorded return time. The restore operation has not yet been tried in the shared environment. If you cannot confirm that the rollback entry still points to the original location, do not continue cleanup or record an untried restore as completed.

At closeout, archive only this borrowing record, the final output, the return time, and the pre-rollback state. If a later window changes the entry or output, keep a separate record; do not overwrite this window's assessment of the missing catalog or the point where rollback stopped.

# ASR-3.0 Freeze Window Q&A

Before the freeze, what kept coming up wasn't implementation detail but three decisions: whether adapter-compat the entry point counts as supported, who withdraws the candidate path, and when the issue can be closed.

**adapter-compat What can the entry point tell us?** The answer at the time was: the entry point is still present, so the compatibility path remains a candidate; that does not by itself mean the entire compatibility surface is supported. The read near the entry point can only count as one observation; it cannot stand in for actual compatibility results.

**Who withdraws the candidate path?** Handle it through the candidate path's maintainer first. If the withdrawal affects existing callers, bring the decision back to the compatibility surface for confirmation. No specific names are listed here.

**Under what conditions can it be closed?** Use the team's usual standard provisionally: `Close a runtime issue only after a positive case, a contrary input, and a follow-up state read agree across the supported compatibility surface.`

The Node runtime transcript with command and exit code has not yet been collected; without it, the issue can only be logged, and the gap cannot be recorded as verified.

# ASR-3.0 Freeze Window FAQ

The easiest thing to misread during the freeze window is "the entry point is still there." After the first review, the earlier claim that the adapter-compat entry point was a support signal needs to be narrowed: it can only show that someone is still following that path to inspect compatibility behavior; it cannot by itself prove that the candidate path can remain on the supported surface.

**What can the adapter-compat entry point tell us?** It can help locate the compatibility path to compare and indicate which object the subsequent state read should target; without a corresponding contrary case for the positive case, no conclusion can be drawn from it.

**Who withdraws the candidate path?** The old answer assigned withdrawal to the path maintainer. The review found that this is only a division of work, not a closure condition. The withdrawal is still initiated by the maintainer, but whether to withdraw depends on the compatibility-surface review; this page does not identify a specific escalation owner.

**Under what conditions can it be closed?** The existing rule still applies: `Close a runtime issue only after a positive case, a contrary input, and a follow-up state read agree across the supported compatibility surface.` all three items must target the same candidate path; do not combine one positive result with the state read from another path.

The Node runtime transcript with command and exit code is still missing. This question has no new answer.

# ASR-3.0 Freeze Window FAQ

This page preserves the answer from the ASR-3.0 freeze period. It was once used as shorthand for withdrawing candidate paths, but field feedback later pointed out that the shorthand conflated "being able to find the entry point" with "being able to retain support." The old answer was not deleted because people still use it to trace back the handling sequence at the time.

**What can the existing adapter-compat entry point prove?** It proves that someone can continue checking along the compatibility path, and can use that to arrange a positive case, contrary input, and subsequent state read. It cannot by itself prove that the path is part of the supported compatibility surface. The old version treated the presence of the entry point as a signal to retain support; that statement no longer applies, but the old judgment was precisely where the later review started.

**Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?** The old position was that the candidate-path maintainer should withdraw it first. The recent correction is: the maintainer Fang Ke carries out the withdrawal, but should not independently treat the withdrawal as grounds for closure. If the three observations of the compatibility surface do not fall on the same candidate path, the withdrawal should remain on hold. This page has never answered who specifically escalates or who approves.

**Under what conditions can it be closed?** The sentence used at the time remains unchanged: `Close a runtime issue only after a positive case, a contrary input, and a follow-up state read agree across the supported compatibility surface.` Here, a positive case is not "the entry point is accessible," and a contrary input is not another ordinary read; together, they must answer the same compatibility assessment. follow-up The state read is used to confirm the state after the operation, not to replace the first two items.

When the Node runtime transcript with command and exit code is missing, the most that can be done is leave the issue on the freeze checklist. Someone previously treated a single local read as grounds for closure; that practice was later withdrawn, but no new runtime record has been added to this page.

See DOC-50 for the single-variable rerun of compatibility-experiment capacity; it does not fill in the runtime record missing from this page.

# Compatibility Experiment Capacity Rerun Log

The two comparison runs still on record are narrow: operation-queue's repository state and call entry points were unchanged, while package revision and caller matrix were logged together as test conditions; only capacity was allowed to change in this round. The old draft treated the first visible divergence as evidence about capacity itself. That was over-attribution at the time; this sentence is retained to explain why the original observation was not replaced by a later summary.

On review, the divergence only indicates that the record reached this round's stopping point; it does not mean the difference has been attributed to capacity. The caller matrix remains part of the fixed conditions, and package revision was merely retained with this round's materials; neither supplies an attribution for the divergence automatically. The freeze coordinator's requirement was copied into the margin at the time, as follows:

> The freeze coordinator accepts only evidence linked to a named card and package revision.

That requirement changes the way evidence is archived; it does not turn the experiment into a conclusion about the queue. The existing materials should separately show the fixed conditions, the sole change, and the stopping point; they cannot be compressed by a post hoc summary into "capacity has been validated." The original results from the first two rounds will continue to be stored separately. Later records may add linkage only; they cannot rewrite what the first round observed.

During the review, the working fields were split into the following items to avoid mixing conditions with judgments again:

- The fixed field records the state of operation-queue, the call entry points, package revision, and caller matrix. These define the boundary of this comparison; they do not explain the capacity difference.
- The variable field lists only capacity. If the caller is changed as well, or other queue parameters are added in the same round, this is no longer the original single-variable record.
- The stopping-point field records only the first visible divergence. Save this round's materials at that point; do not continue from the divergence to add a second capacity value, and do not overwrite it with a later run.
- The linkage field must connect the materials to a named card and package revision. The old record is incomplete here, so the first-round observation cannot stand in for this step.

The old draft's recommendation to "consolidate after the third run" has been withdrawn. It assumed that one more run would consolidate the meaning of the first two rounds, but without linkage, a third run would only add another unattributed observation. The withdrawal does not negate the records from the first round or the review; both remain valuable because they preserve the fact that the repository state, entry points, and caller matrix were not replaced at the time.

The next rerun will still change only capacity. Before starting, first add the linkage between the named card and package revision, then copy the contents of the fixed conditions; after entering through the existing call entry points, stop at the first visible divergence and retain this round's original materials. Do not interpret this stopping point as a general capacity threshold, and do not change the caller matrix in the same rerun to pursue the divergence.

What has not yet been fully collected is which item in the caller matrix is sufficient to serve as the linkage entry point for this divergence. The old page does not identify that item, and the existing records from the two rounds do not fill it in. This gap remains here; turning it into a generalized queue-capacity judgment would change the scope left by this local comparison.

The available material supports the former as the starting point for this round of discussion, but does not establish the entry point's location as the permanent home of the backend, queue, or compatibility layer.

versions.body:
# Maintenance Office Hours Decision Record

These office hours began by separating two actions that are easy to conflate. One was to continue using the current backend-platform entry point for discussions already underway; the other was to adjust the freeze window arrangements. The former determines where to continue examining issues, while the latter determines the pace of handling them during the transition. Both relate to wrapping up this round, but neither can replace the other.

The original draft's "keep the entry point for now" is retained here, but should not be quoted on its own. That sentence was only a working decision at the time: existing discussions could still be tracked from the current entry point, without creating a parallel entry point just for one office hours session. It did not declare any backend to be the only choice, nor did it establish the implementation location near the entry point as the long-term ownership location.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Current backend-platform entry point] --> B[Discussion starting point]
  B --> C[Caller-visible Fang Ke JavaScript behavior]
  C --> D[Same StorageEngine path]
  D --> E[backend]
  D --> F[queue]
  D --> G[compatibility]
```

The lines in the diagram represent the order this decision requires discussions to follow, not an internal call graph. The entry point first provides a starting point from which checks can continue; when making an assessment, first consider the JavaScript behavior visible to callers; then understand related changes involving backend, queue, and compatibility within the same StorageEngine path. Drawing these terms together also does not mean that new implementation conclusions have already been reached for every layer.

## Decisions Made

This round will continue using the current backend-platform entry point for existing issues. This choice has specific benefits: discussions already established around that entry point do not need to move because of window arrangements, and maintainers will not have to maintain two similar explanations with different meanings at the same time. The entry point remains the starting point for discussion, not the endpoint for technical rulings.

Caller-visible Fang Ke JavaScript behavior was adopted as the boundary for assessments in this round. The meeting materials state: "Treat caller-observable JavaScript behavior as the contract, and keep backend, queue, and compatibility changes integrated through one StorageEngine path." Here, contract does not require office hours to supply a complete interface specification; it requires statements about compatibility impacts to be grounded in the behavior callers actually see.

This constraint works in two directions. Assessments based only on backend, queue, or a particular filename cannot automatically become external commitments; conversely, if a caller-visible behavior genuinely requires a joint explanation from the backend, queue, and compatibility layer, those three parts cannot be split into unrelated verbal conclusions. They should be checked together along the shared StorageEngine path.

Office hours therefore approved a narrow line of work, not a new implementation narrative. Work should continue within the scope covered by the existing materials. Implementation guesses not included in those materials may remain as opinions, but cannot acquire certainty merely by appearing in a decision record.

## The Two Approaches Compared at the Time

The proposal to retain the entry point does not claim that the entry point has no problems. It merely acknowledges that existing discussions have already converged there, and moving the entry point cannot by itself fill in the unexplained relationships between backend, queue, and compatibility. If an entry-point change is presented as a structural adjustment, later readers can easily misread "where the discussion starts" as "the internal structure has already been repartitioned." That is precisely the inference this round avoided making.

The proposal to adjust the window also has practical appeal. A transition period often needs a clear cadence, and handling things in a concentrated period looks more decisive than retaining the original entry point. But a window adjustment answers when to handle things, not which behaviors callers already depend on. It can be part of subsequent arrangements, but cannot by itself determine backend selection, queue coordination, or compatibility handling.

The meeting did not adopt the approach of "moving the entire focus of handling to the window." This was not because the window could no longer be adjusted, but because the window cannot replace the behavioral boundary. Without materials connecting the new arrangements to caller-visible behavior, adjusting the window alone would only postpone the articulation of the original technical issue, not make it clearer.

The approach of closing out each layer separately was not adopted either. Listing backend, queue, and compatibility separately may appear to give each term its own conclusion, but in practice loses their connections along the StorageEngine path. Such a split is particularly likely to turn partial impressions into complete assessments: someone sees only the backend entry point and infers that the compatibility layer has already been addressed; someone sees only the queue arrangements and infers that caller-visible results will not change. The existing materials support neither leap.

## Limits on the Scope of Office Hours

The meeting materials include a statement of boundaries: "Office hours cover ownership routing, not undocumented implementation guesses." This does not mean immediately assigning every issue to a fixed person or directory, but routing the discussion back to an entry point capable of continuing the checks. Office hours can identify the scope supported by existing materials and record areas that currently have no answer; they cannot supply a source for undocumented implementation speculation.

This limit explains why "retaining the entry point" is not an ownership decision. An entry point may simply be the easiest place to continue tracking things at present, or the place where existing call relationships converge. Whether it happens to correspond to long-term maintenance ownership is a separate question requiring independent materials. Conflating the two would make a discussion arrangement look like a completed organizational and implementation ruling.

Earlier investigation followed `packages/async-storage/src/runtime/StorageEngine.js` and call names such as backend, queue, and storageengine. This investigation history should be retained because it explains why the discussion began there at the time; however, it gives no additional significance to the file location. Files and call names are clues for locating things, not proof of backend structure, queue relationships, or compatibility responsibilities.

Likewise, implementation guesses raised during office hours do not need to be removed from the record. They can remind later readers where disagreements once existed. The distinction is that the record must keep guesses as guesses, rather than promote them to conclusions on the grounds that "the meeting already discussed them." For this round, what can be approved is the requirement for a behavioral boundary and a shared path, not undocumented internal details.

## Interpretations Corrected After Review

The first correction during review addressed an oversimplification of the initial draft. The draft could easily be read as "since the entry point is being retained, there is no need to discuss the window further." That was not the original decision. The window can still be adjusted, but no adjustment can be described as having resolved compatibility issues or reached a conclusion about caller-visible behavior.

The second interpretation needing correction was "the entry point is retained, so it has all decision-making authority." The original decision did not attach that meaning to the entry point. The entry point is responsible for keeping the discussion from losing context; it is not responsible for absorbing all adjacent changes into a conclusion at one location. Especially when the relationships between the backend, queue, and compatibility layer still need to be checked along the StorageEngine path, the entry point cannot replace that path itself.

The third limit that must be retained is that caller-visible Fang Ke JavaScript behavior is not a slogan that can bypass verification. It rules out assessments based solely on internal terminology, and also requires that changes genuinely affecting callers not be split into several unrelated explanations. The role of office hours is to bring subsequent discussions back to this boundary, not to fill in all the details beyond it.

Understood this way, the decision has not become any less effective. The current entry point remains available; window adjustments are not treated as the default remedy; related changes must remain coherent along the same StorageEngine path. Long-term ownership, specific implementations, and compatibility conclusions unsupported by materials remain unresolved items.

## Relationship to the Transition Handoff

The actual transition handoff for the freeze window is handled by DOC-52. This record does not repeat the handoff process or recast the handoff arrangements as a backend design specification. The two documents retain different things: DOC-52 handles work coordination during window changes; this record preserves the choices made during office hours regarding the entry point, behavioral boundary, and shared path.

If subsequent discussions return to the current entry point, first distinguish whether they concern JavaScript behavior visible to callers or internal guesses about backend, queue, and compatibility. The former can continue to be checked under this decision; the latter should become the subject of a new decision only when they can be placed back on the shared StorageEngine path and sufficient supporting materials become available.

# ASR-3.0 Freeze Cutover Handoff

For the ASR-3.0 freeze window cutover, the handoff unit is not "the candidate module already has code." It is a known consumer leaving the old public entry point, trial-running the candidate path, and being able to return on its own when the result is unclear. batch-contracts is still inventoried at this level of detail. The old entry point remains available during the trial run and must not be removed from the records just because the candidate path is already usable.

The initial draft only said "find a trial user first." After review, this sentence was split into two sequential steps: first count all known consumers, then select one that can roll back on its own for the trial run. Being able to roll back on its own solves where to turn first; it does not mean that the remaining consumers have the same capability.

```text
Before cutover

batch-contracts
    ├── Known consumer list
    │       ├── Trial-run candidate path
    │       ├── Temporarily retain old entry point
    │       └── Pending confirmation
    └── Old public entry point

During cutover

Inventoried consumers ──> One consumer that can roll back on its own ──> Candidate path
        │                         │
        │                         ├── Reproduction artifacts
        │                         └── Rollback action
        └────────────────────────────> Keep the old entry point available

Result

Candidate path can proceed ──> Keep the trial-run record
Candidate path cannot be explained ──> Return to the old entry point and retain the unresolved issue
```

## Establish the migration scope first

Here, "known consumers" does not mean the expected number of people affected, nor potential call sites inferred from a filename. It means consumers that have been confirmed in this round as needing to move away from the old entry point, or as temporarily remaining on the old entry point. Each item must record at least: the public entry point accessed by the consumer, the candidate path it is preparing to use, the module that owns the candidate path, its current handling status, and reproduction artifacts that can be reviewed later.

At minimum, write the statuses separately as "trial run," "temporarily retained on old entry point," "rolled back," and "pending confirmation." "Temporarily retained on old entry point" means that the candidate path has not yet been trial-run; "rolled back" means that it has been trial-run but is currently restored to the old entry point. They must not be combined, or the next person taking over will not know whether to schedule the first trial run or first explain an observed phenomenon.

The inventory should start from the old public entry point. There may already be compatible callers on the candidate-path side, but that is not enough to show that all consumers use the same method. Finding known consumers by the old entry point first, then adding the candidate path item by item, keeps undiscovered, temporarily retained, and migrated consumers separate. Do not mark unconfirmed potential consumers as completed; leave known but not-yet-assessed items as "pending confirmation."

The handoff statement to follow in this round is: `A handoff names the affected public entry point, the owning module, the exact reproduction evidence, and the teammate who can resolve any remaining ambiguity.` These four items belong in every migration item, rather than being used separately as a page-header slogan.

- **Public entry point**: Write the entry point that the consumer is currently leaving. Writing only batch-contracts is not enough, because a scope name cannot indicate the actual path to replace.
- **Owning module**: Write the module that maintains the candidate path. It cannot be inferred solely from the files encountered during the search.
- **Precise reproduction artifacts**: Retain the original artifacts that distinguish the version, environment, and CI job or failure node. The words "passed" or "failed" alone do not let later people determine whether this is the same phenomenon.
- **Person who can resolve ambiguity**: Name a colleague who can explain the consumer's scope, the entry-point relationship, or the rollback action. Do not replace a clear point of contact with "someone knows."

If any of the four is missing, the migration item remains in progress. Without a public entry point, it is unclear what is being migrated; without an owning module, there is no corresponding module to find when the candidate path has a problem; without reproduction artifacts, the result at the time cannot be rechecked; without a clarification contact, the remaining ambiguity will turn into guesswork during the freeze window.

## Select the first item for the trial run

The first item is not selected based on what is "most convenient to modify," but on whether it can roll back on its own. Rolling back on its own means that the consumer can move its integration from the candidate path back to the old public entry point without having to find another module ad hoc to confirm the entry point after the cutover goes wrong. This condition limits the recovery scope of the first cutover; it does not mean that this consumer, Fang Ke, represents all callers.

Before the trial run, write both the old entry point and the candidate path into the item. Do not write only "migrate to the new path," because at the next handoff, "new" will no longer have a stable referent. Also write which module maintains the candidate path and exactly which old entry point to return to if an exception occurs. The consumer's maintainer and the module owning the candidate path may be different; the handoff record does not create a long-term responsibility relationship between them, but it must identify a colleague who can explain any remaining ambiguity.

Retain the original reproduction artifacts during the trial run. The artifacts must include at least the version, environment, and execution node used at the time; if the input contains no existing CI URL, command, or failure node, do not fabricate one. When the artifacts show a failure, first record the entry point, candidate path, and observed behavior; do not directly attribute the cause to a module defect or caller error. When evidence is insufficient, rollback is a handling action, not a cause attribution.

After the trial run, there are only two actions. When the result is sufficient to proceed, retain the item as trial-run and leave the artifacts attached; when the result cannot be explained or recovery cannot be performed reliably, execute the prewritten rollback action and return to the old public entry point. A rolled-back item still belongs to the known scope of batch-contracts; it must not be deleted or rewritten as if it had never been trial-run. The remaining consumers do not automatically become migrated because the first item passed; they must continue to be assessed individually.

## Migration batches and old paths

Do not move all consumers onto the candidate path at once. After the first trial run is complete, the remaining items can be scheduled one by one from the list, but each item still needs its own old entry point, candidate path, owning module, and rollback action. Here, a batch is the processing order for the handoff, not a release batch or date that was not provided in the input; do not invent batch numbers for unconfirmed callers.

The old public entry point has two roles in the cutover record: it is the entry point originally used by the consumer, and it is the recovery location when an exception occurs. It is not thereby designated as the long-term solution. If the candidate path is trial-run again after the artifacts have been completed and ownership clarified, leave a new trial-run record; do not overwrite the new result with the old text saying it was "already tried."

When tracing back through file locations in the past, it was easy to treat the file found as the permanent owner. `packages/async-storage/windows/code/codegen/NativeAsyncStorageModuleSpec.g.h` can still help the next person return to the starting point of this search, but it does not replace the owning module in the handoff item, nor does it indicate which public entry point must be migrated. Generated-file locations and call layouts may change; what this page must retain consistently is the entry point, the candidate path, and their recovery relationship.

## Rollback records

At minimum, leave three things when rolling back: which known consumer was trial-run, which old entry point it returned to from the candidate path, and the reproduction artifacts and unexplained ambiguity at the time. After the rollback action is complete, write the status as "rolled back"; do not write "temporarily retained," and do not mark the candidate path as migrated.

If the artifacts only show that "the candidate path does not work," retain that scope and do not continue guessing at the cause. When the caller's intent, entry-point relationship, or recovery path needs to be explained, assign it to the colleague specified for that item. Until that explanation is available, keep the consumer in the rolled-back or pending-confirmation state. The old entry point is only the current recovery location; it must not be written here as the final solution.

Handoff items may be recorded in the following order; the number of fields does not require copying the entire page:

| Item | Recorded content |
| --- | --- |
| Consumer | The specific caller confirmed in batch-contracts |
| Old entry point | The public entry point currently available for recovery |
| Candidate path | The path to be trial-run or already trial-run |
| Owning module | The module that maintains the candidate path |
| Reproduction artifacts | Version, environment, CI job, or failure-node artifacts |
| Rollback action | The actual action that returns the consumer to the old entry point |
| Clarification contact | The colleague who can explain the remaining issue |
| Current status | Trial run, temporarily retained, rolled back, or pending confirmation |

"Current status" in the table describes only the cutover handoff position, not the release status. It also does not mean that an item has passed all compatibility checks; this page retains only facts about the cutover itself that someone can take over.

## Continue migrating after review

The main gap found in the review was inconsistent recording granularity: some items had only a module name, some had only a caller, and some treated "can roll back" as an assumption that did not need to be written down. Therefore, when adding items later, add the old entry point and candidate path first, then add the owning module, reproduction artifacts, and rollback action. If these details still cannot be confirmed, keep the status as pending confirmation rather than closing with a sentence saying "ready."

DOC-53 can serve as related navigation for the compatibility experiment capacity entry, but it does not replace the migration records on this page. Even if experimental capacity is available, it is still necessary to state which consumer switches from which public entry point to which candidate path, and how to return if it fails.

The freeze-window handoff is still in progress when any of the following occurs:

- Known consumers do not have item-level statuses;
- The trial-run consumer cannot return to the old public entry point within its own scope;
- The reproduction artifacts cannot distinguish the version, environment, or execution node;
- The module owning the candidate path is not clear;
- There is no colleague who can explain the outstanding issue.

Completion does not mean that all consumers immediately leave the old entry point. There may be temporarily retained items and items that have already been rolled back; however, every known consumer must have a clear place in the list, and every item that has been trial-run must retain its entry point, ownership, artifacts, and rollback action. The existence of a candidate path only means that a trial run can be scheduled; it cannot replace the migration status.

# Reading the Code for the Compatibility Lab Capacity Entry Point

When I took over this workstream, I started from the repository's public entry point, test-observability, rather than expanding into every same-named result. I followed one direct caller first, then checked where it handed off the lookup; I stopped only after reaching the first real consumer of compatibility lab capacity. Here, "first" means the next stop along the call edge, not the file that looks most relevant in the search results.

JsonCodec.js is only a signpost in this record. Some same-named files found through filename and call-name searches have no call edge and cannot be treated as actual entry points. An old note treated one of those locations as a consumer; that assessment can now only be retained as historical context. Focusing only on filenames leads in circles among several results; continue checking the references left by the direct caller.

The follow-up check left a Node runtime transcript containing the command actually run and the exit code. It is only for locating this path and is not enough to establish who maintains compatibility lab capacity. After reaching the first consumer, what remained was a collaboration boundary that another owner needs to answer, so I did not continue stitching other pages into a conclusion.
